items.text: Surname: ＿
items.vi: Người gọi đánh vần B-R-A-N-N-I-G-A-N: họ là Brannigan.

audio.t: Good morning, Kestrel Bay Sailing School. How can I help you?
Hello. I saw your advertisement for the adult beginners' weekend, and I'd like to book a place.
Certainly. Could I take your surname first?
It's Brannigan. That's B-R-A-N-N-I-G-A-N.
Thank you, Mr. Brannigan. We run the course on the first weekend of every month, but I'm afraid the one in May is full. The next one starts on the fourteenth of June.
That's fine. What does it cost?

It's two hundred and forty dollars. It was two hundred and sixty last year, but we reduced it. That covers the boat, the instructor and life jackets, but you'll need to bring your own waterproof jacket, because we only supply them in winter.
And what about shoes? I have some hiking boots.
I'd leave those at home. Please wear shoes with soft soles, so that they don't mark the deck. Gloves are useful, but we can lend you a pair.
What sort of boat will we be using?
A small dinghy for two people, called a Wren. Students often ask for a bigger yacht, but you have to learn the basics on the dinghy first.
Where do we meet?

At the boathouse beside the ferry pier, not at the harbor office, which is a common mistake. The first session starts at nine, but please arrive at a quarter to nine so that we can fit your life jacket.
Right. And who will be teaching us?
Ms. Okonkwo. That's O-K-O-N-K-W-O. She has taught beginners here for ten years.
Lovely. Do you need a deposit?
Yes, fifty dollars today, which is refundable if you cancel at least a week before. Could I take a contact number?
Of course. It's five, five, two, oh, eight, one, three.
Five, five, two, oh, eight, one, three. Perfect. I'll send you the details by email as well. We look forward to seeing you in June.

parts.instr: Questions 11-20. Listen to a talk about a heritage railway and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 11-20. Nghe bài nói về một tuyến đường sắt di sản và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Welcome, everyone, to this evening's briefing for new volunteers at the Dunmore Valley Railway. I'm Gareth, the volunteer coordinator, and I'll begin with a little history.

The line opened in 1893. Many people assume it was built for tourists, but it was actually built to carry slate from the quarries down to the port, and passengers were always secondary. It closed in 1961, when the quarries shut, and for twenty years the track lay under brambles.

The revival began in 1982, when a group of former railway employees formed a trust. They were joined by local schoolteachers and engineers, but it was the old employees who knew where everything had been buried. The first two miles reopened in 1984, built almost entirely by volunteers, and we now run seven miles of line.

Our ambition is to reach the village of Carrow, where the old terminus stood. Money is always a worry, but it is not the main obstacle. The real problem is the bridge over the River Aldwen, whose foundations are failing and which must be rebuilt before any train can cross it.

Our pride and joy is Engine Number Six, built in 1924. We found it in a scrapyard abroad in 1997. It took eleven years to restore, and the final bill was nearly three times the original estimate, which is a lesson in how restorations go.

Unfortunately, you won't see her running next winter. The boiler has to be inspected thoroughly every ten years, and the next inspection is due in January, so she will be out of service until the spring. Don't worry, though, because our diesel locomotive will pull the trains.

Now, to you. We have many jobs for volunteers: signaling, carriage restoration, catering and track maintenance. Most newcomers choose the catering team, because it is warm and sociable. Signaling is popular too, though it takes training. But our greatest shortage is in track maintenance. It is heavy work, in all weather, and we simply cannot find enough people.
You don't need any experience, but everyone must complete our two-day safety course before they work anywhere near moving trains. A first aid certificate is useful, but it is not compulsory.
In return, we can't pay wages, but all volunteers travel free on our trains and receive a uniform. Those who give a hundred hours or more in a year also get a free family membership.

Finally, our next open day is on the first Saturday of October. We expect about two thousand visitors, so new volunteers will mostly be asked to help with parking and to direct people to the station. It's a good way to meet everyone. Now, are there any questions?

items.q: Why was the Dunmore Valley line originally built?
options: to transport slate to the port
to bring tourists to the coast
items.vi: Tuyến được xây để chở đá phiến ra cảng; hành khách chỉ là phụ.

items.q: Who started the revival of the railway?
items.vi: Những cựu nhân viên đường sắt lập quỹ tín thác; giáo viên và kỹ sư chỉ tham gia sau.

items.q: What is the main obstacle to extending the line to Carrow?
options: a bridge that has to be rebuilt
items.vi: Vấn đề chính là cây cầu qua sông Aldwen có móng yếu; tiền chỉ là mối lo thứ yếu.

items.q: How long did it take to restore Engine Number Six?
items.vi: Mất 11 năm để phục chế đầu máy; chi phí gần gấp ba dự toán.

items.q: Why will Engine Number Six be out of service next winter?
options: Its boiler needs to be inspected.
It needs a new paint job.
The diesel locomotive is replacing it.
items.vi: Nồi hơi phải kiểm tra mười năm một lần, đến hạn vào tháng Một.

items.q: In which area does the railway most need volunteers?
items.vi: Thiếu người nhất ở bảo trì đường ray vì việc nặng, làm ngoài trời mọi thời tiết.

items.q: What must all volunteers do before working near moving trains?
items.vi: Mọi tình nguyện viên phải học khóa an toàn hai ngày; chứng chỉ sơ cứu không bắt buộc.

items.q: What do all volunteers receive in return for their work?
items.vi: Tất cả được đi tàu miễn phí và nhận đồng phục; thẻ gia đình chỉ dành cho người làm từ 100 giờ.

items.q: How many visitors do the organizers expect at the open day?
items.vi: Dự kiến khoảng hai nghìn khách tham quan.

items.q: What will new volunteers mostly do at the open day?
items.vi: Người mới chủ yếu giúp đỗ xe và chỉ đường tới nhà ga.

parts.instr: Questions 21-30. Listen to two students talking to their tutor and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 21-30. Nghe hai sinh viên nói chuyện với giáo viên và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your dialect project.
Yes, Dr. Hale. We've decided to record older fishermen in the harbor town of Pellmouth, and to collect the words they use for tools and for weather.
I'm worried that six people is too small a sample. They were the only ones willing to take part.

Six can be acceptable for a qualitative study, provided you explain how you found them. My concern is different. If they all belong to the same crew and drink in the same pub, they may share one vocabulary, and you'd mistake that for the town's.
That's true. We did think about using a questionnaire first, but Karim preferred interviews.
People talk much more naturally when you ask them in person. Though I suppose they may change how they speak because of the recorder.
Linguists call that the observer's paradox. One way round it is to ask them to tell stories, about storms or accidents for example, so that they forget the microphone.
We'd also planned to use software that turns speech into text, to save us typing.

I'd be careful. Automatic transcription copes badly with regional accents and old-fashioned words, so you'd spend as long correcting it as typing it yourselves. I'd transcribe a few minutes by hand first.
What about the ethics form?
You need written consent from every participant, and the form must state that they can withdraw at any time. Some may not want their names published, so offer to use initials instead.
We thought of including a map showing where each word is used.
Maps look impressive, but with six speakers they can mislead. I think a table comparing each word with its entry in an older dictionary would be more convincing.
When do you need the draft?
By the tenth of March. The final report is due on the twenty-fourth. I know the third of March is the end of term, but don't confuse the dates.
Could we borrow a recorder from the department? Our phones aren't good in noisy places.
I'll ask the technician to lend you a professional one. It has to be booked in advance, so I'll do that this afternoon.
Thank you. I think we should run a practice interview with my grandfather first.
Excellent idea. Send me the recording and I'll give you some feedback before you start properly.

items.q: What is the tutor's main concern about the sample?
options: Six people is far too few.
The participants may not speak honestly.
The participants may all use the same vocabulary.
items.vi: Thầy lo vì các ngư dân cùng một nhóm sẽ dùng chung từ vựng, và sinh viên sẽ nhầm đó là từ vựng của cả thị trấn.

items.q: Why does Karim prefer interviews to a questionnaire?
items.vi: Karim cho rằng nói trực tiếp thì người ta tự nhiên hơn.

items.q: What does the tutor suggest to reduce the observer's paradox?
options: asking the participants to tell stories
items.vi: Kể chuyện (bão, tai nạn) khiến họ quên micro.

items.q: What is the tutor's opinion of speech-to-text software?
options: It is too expensive for students.
It produces words that are hard to read.
It is unreliable with regional accents.
It saves a great deal of time.
items.vi: Phần mềm xử lý kém giọng địa phương và từ cổ nên sửa lỗi tốn thời gian như tự gõ.

items.q: What must the consent form say?
options: Participants will be paid for their time.
All recordings will be destroyed afterward.
Participants can leave the study whenever they wish.
items.vi: Biểu mẫu phải nêu rõ người tham gia được rút lui bất cứ lúc nào.

items.q: What does the tutor suggest for participants who do not want to be named?

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at the intelligence of octopuses, animals whose ancestors split from ours more than five hundred million years ago. In a sense they are the nearest thing we have to an intelligent alien on our own planet.

An octopus has roughly five hundred million neurons, about the same as a dog. What is remarkable is where they are. Only a third are in the central brain; two thirds are in the arms. Each arm can taste and touch, and it can make simple decisions without consulting the brain, which is why an arm cut off from the body can still react to a stimulus.

Their problem solving is well documented. In laboratories, octopuses have learned to unscrew a jar from the inside to reach the food in it, and one famous individual repeatedly escaped from its tank at night to eat crabs in a neighboring one. In the wild, the veined octopus collects coconut shells, carries them across the seabed and assembles them into a shelter. That is tool use in the strict sense, because the shells are carried before they are needed.

How do they learn? Mainly by trial and error, and they can certainly tell shapes and patterns apart. An early experiment suggested that they could also learn by watching other octopuses, but later researchers failed to repeat it, so the evidence for observational learning is weak.

There is a puzzle here. Many species live for only a year or two, and the females die soon after their eggs hatch. Hatchlings therefore never meet their parents, so there is no opportunity for knowledge to be passed on. Their intelligence is individual, not cultural, which is very different from crows or chimpanzees.

Now to camouflage. An octopus changes color in a fraction of a second, using thousands of elastic color cells in the skin called chromatophores, that's C-H-R-O-M-A-T-O-P-H-O-R-E-S. Yet most species appear to be color-blind, which is odd. One hypothesis is that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself help them detect the color of their surroundings.

Finally, a word on ethics. Because of this evidence of intelligence and apparent pain, several countries have now included octopuses and their relatives in animal welfare laws, which means that experiments on them need approval. Next week we will look at how that approval process works.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 1: The creative brain. Answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 1. Trả lời câu 1-13.

items.text:
A
For centuries, creativity was attributed to divine inspiration or to an elusive spark of genius, and it was assumed to live in a single hemisphere of the brain. The popular notion that artists are "right-brained" and engineers "left-brained" persists in classrooms and magazines, yet neuroscientists regard it as a myth. Imaging studies of musicians, poets and mathematicians solving open-ended problems show activity distributed across both hemispheres, and no region that could be called the seat of imagination. Contemporary research instead treats creativity as an emergent property of networks, that is, of the coordinated behavior of widely separated areas, and asks which networks matter and how they cooperate. This shift in emphasis mirrors a wider change in neuroscience, which increasingly regards complex abilities such as language, memory and planning as products of interaction rather than of isolated centers. It also makes the question harder to answer, because a network cannot be located by pointing to a single bright patch on a scan.

B
The first large-scale clue came from an unexpected direction. In the early 2000s, researchers noticed that when volunteers lay in a scanner with nothing to do, a particular set of regions became more active rather than less. This "default mode network", which includes parts of the medial prefrontal cortex and the posterior cingulate, supports mind-wandering, autobiographical memory and the imagining of future scenes. Because creative thought often begins with loosely associated ideas drifting into awareness, scientists hypothesized that this network supplies the raw material. Participants who score highly on tests of divergent thinking, such as listing unusual uses for a brick, tend to show stronger connectivity within it.

C
Raw material is not enough, however. A second system, the executive control network, centered on the lateral prefrontal cortex, evaluates ideas, suppresses the obvious and keeps attention on a goal. In most tasks the default and control networks behave like rivals, one rising as the other falls. A study led by the neuroscientist Mirela Voss at the Halden Institute found that professional designers, when generating concepts, showed both networks active at the same time, a pattern rare in non-experts. Creative expertise may therefore lie less in having wilder ideas than in the capacity to let generation and judgment operate together, with a third "salience network" switching attention between the two as needed.

D
Chemistry modulates this traffic. Dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with reward and exploration, has been linked to flexible thinking, and people with moderately higher dopamine receptor availability in certain regions tend to produce more original responses. Yet the relationship is not linear. Too little leaves thinking rigid, but too much, as in some psychotic conditions, loosens associations to the point of incoherence. This inverted-U pattern helps explain why creativity and mental illness are statistically linked in some populations without the former being a symptom of the latter: most creative people are healthy, and extreme states usually impair productive work rather than enhance it. Researchers add that dopamine is only one of several chemical messengers involved, and that its effects depend on the region of the brain in which it acts, so that no simple pill or diet could be expected to switch originality on.

E
The famous "aha" moment has also been studied. When volunteers solve word puzzles through sudden insight rather than step-by-step reasoning, EEG recordings show a burst of high-frequency gamma activity in the right anterior temporal lobe about three hundred milliseconds before they report the answer. This is preceded by a brief rise in alpha waves over the visual cortex, which is interpreted as the brain momentarily shutting out distracting input. Insight, in other words, appears to be prepared by quiet internal work that the person does not experience. This may explain the common experience of solutions arriving in the shower, or after sleep, when attention is relaxed. In experiments in which participants slept after being given a hard problem, those who entered rapid-eye-movement sleep were more likely to spot a hidden rule on waking.

F
Such findings have practical implications, but researchers urge caution. Brain stimulation devices marketed to boost creativity have produced inconsistent results, and many imaging studies involve small samples and artificial tasks that bear little resemblance to writing a novel or designing a bridge. Moreover, creativity is not a single ability: the cognitive demands of improvising jazz differ from those of devising a mathematical proof. Most scientists therefore see the field as young. What seems secure is a broader lesson, that creative ideas arise from cooperation among systems rather than from any one gifted organ, and that the conditions which nurture them, such as rest, freedom to wander and tolerance of error, can be cultivated by ordinary people. Whether such conditions can be reproduced in a classroom or an office remains an open question for future studies.

items.q: Which paragraph describes a chemical influence that can both help and harm thinking?

items.vi: Đoạn F: thiết bị kích thích não cho kết quả không nhất quán, mẫu nhỏ, nhiệm vụ nhân tạo.

items.q: Which paragraph suggests why ideas may arrive when people are relaxed?

items.q: What is the writer's main point in paragraph A?
options: Artists and engineers use their brains in different ways.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 2: Carbon beneath our feet. Answer questions 14-26.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 2. Trả lời câu 14-26.

items.text:
A
Soils hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all the world's vegetation combined: roughly 2,500 billion tonnes in the top two meters, according to commonly cited estimates. The figure matters because small changes in so large a store can have large consequences. Since agriculture began, ploughing and the clearing of natural vegetation have caused cultivated soils to lose perhaps a quarter to a half of their original carbon, which has passed into the air as carbon dioxide. Natural ecosystems, by contrast, tend to build carbon slowly over many centuries, since plant growth and decomposition remain roughly in balance. It has therefore seemed logical to propose that farmland, having been a source, could become a sink, and in 2015 an initiative launched by the French government promoted the idea that raising soil carbon by four parts per thousand each year could offset a substantial share of human emissions.

B
The biology is straightforward. Plants draw carbon dioxide from the air and convert it into sugars. A portion is exuded through roots to feed fungi and bacteria, and when plants and microbes die their remains build up organic matter. Contrary to older textbooks, the most durable carbon is not the coarse, woody litter that accumulates on the surface, but compounds produced by microbes and bound to fine mineral particles, where they are physically shielded from decomposers. This revision has shifted attention from simply adding biomass to supporting living soil communities and the mineral surfaces on which carbon can be stabilized.

C
Several farming practices are known to raise soil carbon: planting cover crops between harvests, rotating deep-rooted perennials with annual grains, reducing tillage, and integrating livestock through managed grazing. Results vary widely, however. In the long-running Ardmore trials, converting to no-till farming raised carbon in the upper ten centimeters at most sites, yet showed little net change when deeper layers were sampled, because tillage often redistributes carbon through the soil profile rather than destroying it. Critics argue that many early claims for no-till were inflated precisely because only the surface was measured, and that the benefits of each practice depend heavily on climate, soil texture and the crops grown. A method that works well on the heavy clay soils of a cool, wet region may do little on sandy soils in a hot one, which makes it risky to extrapolate from a single trial to a national program.

D
Permanence is a second difficulty. Carbon accumulates quickly at first but approaches a new equilibrium within twenty to fifty years, after which a field can hold no more. Worse, the store is reversible: a single return to deep ploughing, a severe drought, or a warmer climate that accelerates microbial respiration can release decades of accumulation within a few seasons. A forest can be protected by law, whereas a farmer's field is managed by a tenant who may change crops with the market. For this reason soil carbon is best regarded as a limited and temporary contribution to climate goals, rather than a permanent solution to emissions.

E
Measurement presents a third obstacle. Soil carbon varies enormously within a single field, so detecting a change of a few tenths of a percent requires many samples collected at the same locations and depths, then analyzed in laboratories at considerable cost. Remote sensing and spectral methods are improving, but they are not yet accurate enough to certify credits. This matters because carbon markets pay farmers for each tonne stored. If payments are made on estimates from computer models rather than from measurement, they may reward practices that would have been adopted anyway, or overestimate gains. Several auditing studies have found that a significant proportion of credits were issued for storage that would have happened regardless.

F
Yet the case for building soil carbon does not rest on climate alone. Organic matter improves the ability of soil to retain water, supports yields in dry years and can reduce the need for fertilizer. Farmers in the semi-arid Karrow Valley who adopted cover crops reported steadier harvests and lower input costs even where carbon gains were modest. Many scientists therefore urge that soil carbon be presented as a co-benefit of resilient farming, not as a commodity to be traded. In this view, the practical aim is not to chase a number of tonnes but to keep land covered, rooted and biologically active, and to regard any carbon removed from the atmosphere as a welcome by-product rather than the justification. Such a modest framing may seem less exciting to investors and politicians, but it has the advantage of being honest about what the soil can and cannot deliver.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 3: Measuring the day. Answer questions 27-40.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 3. Trả lời câu 27-40.

items.text:
A
For most of human history, time was local and elastic. Sundials divided daylight into twelve hours, which meant that an hour in summer was substantially longer than one in winter, and the Egyptians and Romans accepted the variation without complaint because there was little to coordinate beyond dawn, market and sunset. Water clocks, or clepsydrae, allowed measurement at night and indoors, and they were used in Athenian courts to limit the length of speeches. But their flow rate shifted with temperature and with the pressure of the water, and none could be trusted for more than a rough count.

B
Medieval monasteries created the first real demand for regularity. The Benedictine rule required prayer at fixed canonical hours, and by the thirteenth century European craftsmen had devised the mechanical escapement, a device that releases a falling weight in small, equal steps. The earliest tower clocks had no faces and simply struck bells; indeed, the English word clock derives from a medieval word for bell. Their accuracy was poor, often losing or gaining a quarter of an hour in a day, but towns adopted them eagerly once they discovered that a public bell could organize markets, wages and curfews, whatever the exact minute.

C
A leap in precision followed Galileo's observation that a pendulum swings at a rate nearly independent of the width of its arc. In 1656 Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, reducing typical errors from minutes to seconds a day. The balance spring, introduced for portable watches a few years later, brought comparable gains in principle, though pocket watches remained expensive and unreliable for another century. For the first time, ordinary households in prosperous towns could own an instrument that could divide the day into minutes, and the minute hand began to appear on clock faces.

D
The sea demanded the greatest accuracy. To calculate longitude, a navigator needs to know the time at a fixed reference point. Because the Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour, an error of four minutes means an error of one degree, about sixty nautical miles near the equator, which is the difference between a safe harbor and a reef. Pendulum clocks were useless on a pitching ship. After a series of disastrous wrecks, the British government offered a large prize in 1714, and the self-taught clockmaker John Harrison spent decades producing a series of marine timekeepers, the fourth of which lost only a few seconds during nearly three months at sea in 1761 and 1762. The authorities, nevertheless, were slow to reward him, and he was paid in installments.

E
The railways forced a different kind of agreement. Before the 1840s, each English town kept its own local solar time, so that noon in Bristol arrived some ten minutes after noon in London. Timetables became confusing when trains ran across these differences, and the companies adopted a single "railway time" set from Greenwich and transmitted by telegraph. In North America, with its continental distances, railroads imposed four standard time zones in 1883. An international conference in Washington the following year chose the Greenwich meridian as the world's prime meridian, although France abstained and continued to use Paris time for some years afterward. Standardization, in other words, was a matter of negotiation, not of science alone.

F
Twentieth-century physics replaced the spinning Earth as the standard. Quartz crystals, which vibrate at a stable frequency when electrified, brought cheap accuracy to wristwatches from the 1960s. Then came atomic clocks: in 1967 the second was redefined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation emitted by the caesium-133 atom. Modern optical clocks based on strontium are so stable that they would lose less than a second over a period longer than the age of the universe. Because the Earth's rotation is irregular, leap seconds have been added occasionally to keep civil time aligned with daylight, an arrangement that engineers dislike because it can cause computer failures. International metrologists have voted to phase it out by 2035.

G
Accurate time now underpins much of modern life, often invisibly. Satellite navigation works by comparing the signals of clocks aboard satellites, so that a timing error of a billionth of a second translates into a position error of about thirty centimeters. Financial exchanges timestamp transactions to the microsecond, and power grids and mobile networks synchronize with atomic reference signals. Historians point to an irony: as clocks have become ever more precise, human experience of time has not necessarily become calmer. Sociologists associate the spread of clock discipline with industrial work, and surveys suggest that many people feel more rushed than their grandparents did, despite devices that save time. Precision, it seems, has changed what we ask of the hour as much as how we measure it.

parts.instr: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of all journeys made by different forms of transport in the city of Aldport in 2004 and in 2022.

Walking: 18 percent (2004), 22 percent (2022)
Cycling: 6 percent, 14 percent
Bus: 24 percent, 17 percent
Car: 46 percent, 32 percent
Train and metro: 6 percent, 15 percent
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the share of journeys made by five forms of transport in Aldport in 2004 and 2022. Overall, car use fell considerably while the less polluting options, especially trains and bicycles, became far more popular.

In 2004 the car was by far the most common choice, accounting for 46 percent of all journeys, almost double the share of the bus, which came second at 24 percent. Walking made up 18 percent, whereas cycling and the train and metro were each used for only 6 percent of trips.

By 2022 the picture had changed noticeably. The proportion of journeys by car dropped by 14 percentage points to 32 percent, although it remained the single largest category. The bus also declined, to 17 percent. In contrast, the train and metro rose from 6 to 15 percent, an increase of more than double, and cycling grew from 6 to 14 percent. Walking increased more modestly, from 18 to 22 percent.

In summary, Aldport residents moved away from cars and buses toward rail, bicycles and walking, although the car stayed the most popular way to travel.
items.vi: Task 1: nêu xu hướng chung (xe hơi giảm, tàu/xe đạp tăng), so sánh các số liệu chính của 2004 và 2022 với số liệu cụ thể.

parts.instr: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Bạn nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people believe that governments should spend public money on space exploration, while others think that this money should be used to solve problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether governments should fund space exploration or concentrate on problems on Earth. In my opinion, both views have merit, but a modest and carefully planned space budget is justified.

Those who oppose spending on space point to urgent needs at home. Millions of people lack clean water, adequate housing or basic healthcare, and a single space mission can cost as much as a national vaccination program. It seems difficult to defend launching a telescope while hospitals in the same country are short of nurses. Critics also argue that the benefits of space research are uncertain and often reach only wealthy nations.

However, supporters of space programs make a strong case too. Many technologies that we now take for granted, such as satellite weather forecasting, global navigation and certain medical imaging techniques, grew out of space research. Satellites also monitor deforestation, sea levels and pollution, which means that looking outward can actually help us to protect our own planet. In addition, ambitious projects inspire young people to study science and engineering, and these skills benefit the whole economy.

Moreover, the two aims are not really in competition. Space agencies usually receive only a tiny fraction of national budgets, far less than health, education or defense. Cutting them entirely would release little money, whereas the knowledge they produce can last for generations.

In conclusion, governments should not abandon space exploration, but they should set clear priorities and make sure that programs deliver practical benefits. If funding for poverty and health is protected first, a small investment in space is a sensible long-term decision.
items.vi: Task 2: thảo luận hai quan điểm (chi cho vũ trụ và giải quyết vấn đề trên Trái đất), nêu ý kiến riêng, có mở bài và kết luận rõ ràng.

items.q: Describe a piece of music that is important to you. You should say: what it is, when you first heard it, how often you listen to it, and explain why it is important to you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a piano piece that is very important to me, a gentle melody that my grandmother used to play on an old upright piano. I first heard it when I was about seven years old. I remember sitting on the floor beside her one rainy afternoon while she played it slowly, and I was surprised that something so simple could make the whole room feel calm. After that, I asked her to play it whenever I visited. These days I listen to it quite often, usually in the evening on my phone, especially when I am stressed about exams or work. Sometimes I even try to play it myself, although I am not very good, and I still make a lot of mistakes in the middle section. The reason it is so important to me is that it reminds me of her and of a happy period in my childhood. My grandmother passed away a few years ago, but when I hear the music I feel as if she is still nearby. It also taught me that music does not have to be complicated to be powerful. A few simple notes, played with feeling, can be remembered for a lifetime.
items.vi: Mô tả một bản nhạc: tên, lần đầu nghe, tần suất nghe và vì sao quan trọng; nói trôi chảy trong khoảng hai phút.

items.q: Why do you think music is important in every culture?
items.sample: I think music is important in every culture because it expresses emotions that people cannot always put into words. It also brings people together at celebrations, ceremonies and festivals, so it helps communities to feel connected and to pass traditions on to the next generation.
items.vi: Giải thích vai trò của âm nhạc: biểu đạt cảm xúc, gắn kết cộng đồng, truyền thống.

items.q: Should schools make music lessons compulsory for all students?

audio.t: Good morning, Starfield Retreat Centre, Anna speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book places on your Dark Sky Weekend, please.
Certainly. Can I take your surname first?
It's Brennick. That's B-R-E-N-N-I-C-K.
Thank you, Mr Brennick. And a contact number?
Yes, my office number is five five five, zero one eight seven. Oh, but you'd better take my mobile, because I'm away from the office all week. That's five five five, zero one four two.
Five five five, zero one four two. Lovely. How many people is the booking for?
Four adults. My wife and I, and her brother and his partner. My daughter wanted to come as well, but she's away that weekend, so just the four of us.
Fine. We have places on the fourteenth of March and on the fourth of April.
April is a bit late for us, because the sky will be too light in the evenings. The fourteenth of March, then.
Good choice. Now, rooms. We have doubles, twins and a family room.
My brother-in-law and his partner would like a double. My wife and I prefer separate beds, so a twin room for us, please.
No problem. The price is normally ninety-five dollars per person for the weekend, but because you are booking before the end of January, it comes down to eighty-five.
That's good news. Is that with meals?
Yes, all meals are included. Does anybody have special dietary needs?
My wife and I eat anything, but my brother-in-law's partner is vegetarian.

That's fine, our chef is very good with vegetarian dishes. Now, a tip. On Saturday night you will be outside for hours, and it gets very cold, so bring warm clothes. Also bring a torch, but cover it with a red filter. White light ruins your night vision, and other guests will not thank you for it.
I'll remember that. Do you sell the filters?
We do, but a red torch works equally well. Next, there's a workshop on Saturday afternoon. You can choose between telescope making and astrophotography.
Oh, astrophotography, definitely. My wife has just bought a new camera and she's desperate to try it.
Excellent. The last thing is parking. There is a fee of six dollars per car for the weekend, paid on arrival. It was five last year, I'm afraid.
That's fine. We'll come in one car.
Then that's everything, Mr Brennick. I'll send you a confirmation by email today.

Four adults. My wife and I, and her brother and his partner. My daughter wanted to come as well, but she's away that weekend, so just the four of us.
Fine. We have places on the fourteenth of March and on the fourth of April.

My wife and I eat anything, but my brother-in-law's partner is vegetarian.

That's fine. We'll come in one car.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a new community tool library and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về một thư viện dụng cụ cộng đồng mới và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the opening night of the Cranmere Tool Library. My name is Dana Okafor and I chair the volunteer committee. I'd like to explain how we got here, how the library works, and how you can help.

The idea came up two years ago at a street party on Willow Lane. One neighbour mentioned that she had bought an expensive drill, used it for twenty minutes, and then left it in a cupboard. Someone suggested a bike scheme, someone else a book swap, but it was the drill story that made us laugh, and then think.

We first tried lending from a garden shed, but it flooded in the winter, so we spent a year looking for a proper home. The old bakery on Mill Street was the obvious choice, though the owner wanted a high rent. In the end the credit union next door let us have its ground floor free for three years, in exchange for putting up its sign.

Membership costs twelve dollars a year, or six dollars for students and retired people. Some people expected it to be free, but the fee covers insurance, which was our biggest worry. Each member can borrow up to three items at a time, for a week, and there is a late fee of one dollar a day, which we donate to the repair workshop at the community centre.

We now have about four hundred items. The most popular are the ladder, the pressure washer and the wallpaper stripper. Surprisingly, the sewing machines have not been borrowed once, although we think that is because nobody knows they are here, so please tell your friends.

Most tools were donated, and each one is checked by a volunteer before it goes on the shelf. We can't accept anything that has lost its safety guard, however cheap it looks, and we don't take chemicals of any kind. Electrical items also need a safety certificate, which Mr Lindqvist, a retired electrician, gives us free of charge.

On the first Saturday of each month we run a skills session, where someone shows how to tile a wall or fix a leaking tap. Last month we had thirty people at the tiling session, but only eight at the plumbing one, which we put down to the weather rather than the topic, because it was the first sunny weekend of the spring.

Now, volunteering. We need people for the desk on weekday evenings, and the shortage is greatest on Thursdays. Monday and Wednesday are covered, and Friday is quiet anyway. You don't need to know anything about tools. Training takes one evening, and we will provide it next Tuesday, not this Thursday as it says on the leaflet, which was printed before the plan changed.

options: A plan to start a book swap
A neighbour's drill that was hardly ever used
A proposal for a bicycle scheme
A survey carried out by the council

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor about a survey project and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư về một dự án khảo sát và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your survey project.
Yes, Dr Hale. We're investigating attitudes to the proposed tidal power scheme at Port Eskew.
Good. Why Port Eskew? I'd have expected you to choose a scheme that already exists.
We thought about that, because there is one near my hometown. But then people would be describing their experience, and we wanted their expectations, before anything is built.
Also, the town is quite divided. The council says the scheme will bring jobs, but some residents worry about the birds on the estuary.
That's a sensible reason. Now, your draft questionnaire. Look at question four: Do you agree that clean tidal energy is the best way to protect our children's future?
We wanted it to sound positive.
That's exactly the trouble. It is a leading question. It pushes the respondent towards one answer, and the wording would make anyone who disagrees seem selfish. Keep the wording neutral.
Understood. Next, the sample. We were thinking of getting fifty responses.
Too few. You want to compare age groups, and fifty split four ways is nothing. Aim for at least one hundred and twenty.
In two weeks? That will be hard.
We planned to post the link on local social media groups.
That will reach younger residents, but you will miss many older people, whose views are probably the most relevant to a long-term scheme.
We could run a stall at the weekly market as well, with paper copies.
Yes, do both. Now, did you pilot the questionnaire?
With five friends. Most of them were confused by question seven, because we had used the phrase energy yield.
Then replace it with plain language, such as how much electricity the scheme will produce. Nobody should need a dictionary to answer.
There's another problem. The fishing community will be affected most, but there are only a few fishers, so the survey will hardly include them.
Then don't rely on the survey for them. Arrange three or four short interviews with fishers separately.
Right. And about ethics, we planned to ask for names so we could enter people in a prize draw.
Then put the draw entry on a separate form, so the answers stay anonymous. Also add a short consent statement at the top of the questionnaire.
We'll do that. For the results, we were going to use pie charts.
For one question, perhaps. But to compare age groups, bar charts show differences much more clearly.
Is there anything you like in the proposal?
Yes. The strongest part is your research question. It is narrow and it can really be answered. Your literature review is thinner, so spend a little time on that.
When do you need the revised questionnaire? Friday?
I'm away on Friday. Send it by Wednesday of next week, and I'll reply within two days.

items.q: Why did the students choose Port Eskew for their survey?
options: The council asked them to investigate
They wanted opinions before the scheme was built
A similar scheme already operates there
items.vi: Họ muốn biết kỳ vọng của người dân trước khi dự án được xây.

items.q: What does Dr Hale criticise about question four?

audio.t: Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the most elegant examples of self-organisation in nature, the sand dune.

Dunes only start to form when the wind passes a minimum value, known as the threshold speed. Below it, the grains stay where they are. Above it, they begin to move, and the strength of the wind decides how much sand is carried.

Grains travel in three ways. The finest dust is suspended in the air and may cross oceans. The coarsest grains simply creep along the ground, pushed by their neighbours. But most movement, around three quarters, is saltation, in which grains bounce along the surface in short hops, knocking other grains loose when they land.

A dune grows when sand is trapped where the wind slows down, for example behind a rock or a plant. The windward side is a gentle slope, and sand is pushed up it until it reaches the crest. Beyond the crest the air is sheltered, and the sand spills down the lee side, called the slip face. This face always settles at about thirty-four degrees, known as the angle of repose. Any steeper, and the sand avalanches.
Where sand is limited and the wind blows from one direction, the result is a barchan, a dune shaped like a crescent, with its horns pointing downwind.

Dunes migrate. Smaller dunes move faster than large ones, because less sand needs to be shifted to move the crest forward. A barchan about ten metres high may move about twenty metres in a year, while a giant dune a hundred metres high may travel only two metres in the same time.

Some dunes make sound. Singing dunes produce a deep hum, close to one hundred hertz, that can be heard kilometres away. It happens only when the sand is dry and the grains are rounded and of similar size. Damp sand is silent.

Dunes are not unique to Earth. Satellite images show them on Mars, but the atmosphere there is about one per cent as dense as ours, so winds must be very strong to move the grains, and Martian dunes shift only slowly.

Finally, a practical point. In many desert countries, moving dunes bury roads and railways, and they also threaten farmland and villages. Engineers use computer models of dune migration to decide where to put fences and plant vegetation. The first priority is usually the roads, ahead of farmland and villages.

items.text:
A
When Alexander Fleming accepted his Nobel Prize in 1945, he used part of his speech to issue a warning. It was not difficult, he said, to make microbes resistant to penicillin in a laboratory by exposing them to amounts too small to kill them, and the same thing could happen in the body of a patient who took too little of the drug for too short a time. The warning was largely ignored. Antibiotics seemed to have turned infectious disease into a problem of the past, and for several decades pharmaceutical companies introduced new classes of drug faster than bacteria could learn to evade them. That period of comfortable confidence is now over. The World Health Organization counts antimicrobial resistance among the greatest threats to global health, and a widely cited review commissioned by the British government estimated that, without action, drug-resistant infections could cause ten million deaths a year by 2050. Such projections are inevitably uncertain, but few specialists dispute their general direction.

B
Resistance is not a modern invention. It is a consequence of natural selection, and it is older than medicine. Bacteria have been competing with fungi and with one another for billions of years, and many antibiotics are simply weapons that microorganisms evolved to use against rivals; the genes that defend against them evolved in parallel. Researchers who sequenced DNA from permafrost sediment more than thirty thousand years old found genes conferring resistance to several modern drugs. What human activity has changed is the selective pressure. In any large population of bacteria, a few individuals carry mutations that allow them to survive a given drug. When the drug is applied, the susceptible majority die and the rare survivors multiply into the space left behind. The more often and the more widely antibiotics are used, the more often this sorting takes place.

C
Bacteria also have a means of spreading resistance that has no counterpart in animals: they can exchange genes directly. Through a process called horizontal gene transfer, a bacterium can pass a small ring of DNA, known as a plasmid, to a neighbour, even one of a different species. A single plasmid may carry resistance to several unrelated drugs, so that a bacterium acquiring it becomes resistant to all of them at once. Dr Ilse Moravec, a microbiologist at the Halvorsen Institute, compares plasmids to software updates passed between strangers on a train, and points out that the process works fastest in crowded environments such as hospital wards, sewage systems and intensive livestock sheds. She has described the hospital sink drain as the busiest marketplace in medicine, although she accepts that the evidence for how often transfer occurs there is still thin.

D
Misuse of antibiotics speeds the process. In many countries, doctors still prescribe them for viral illnesses such as colds, against which they are useless, often because patients expect a prescription. In others, the drugs can be bought without one, and people take them in the wrong dose or for the wrong condition. The traditional advice to complete every course, even after symptoms vanish, is also being reconsidered. The advice was meant to prevent partly treated infections from returning, but a number of trials suggest that shorter courses work just as well for many common infections, and that prolonged exposure may give resistant bacteria more time to emerge. Specialists stress that this does not mean patients should stop treatment when they feel like it; the right length should be set by research and by the doctor, not guessed by the patient.

E
Medicine is not the only source of pressure. In several countries, more antibiotics by weight are given to farm animals than to people, often to make them grow faster or to prevent disease in crowded conditions rather than to treat sick animals. Resistant bacteria can reach humans through meat, through the environment and through farm workers. The European Union banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in 2006. Denmark, which had restricted the practice several years earlier, managed to reduce its total animal consumption of antibiotics without large losses in productivity, though critics note that farmers there partly substituted other medicines and improved hygiene at the same time, so the lessons are difficult to separate. What the Danish example does show is that high use is not an unavoidable cost of intensive farming.

F
Even if the pressure were removed tomorrow, the world would still need new drugs, and here economics gets in the way. A new antibiotic is deliberately held in reserve, used only when older drugs fail, and then prescribed for a week or two. Compare that with a medicine for diabetes or high blood pressure, which patients take every day for decades. The result is that a successful antibiotic may earn too little to repay the cost of developing it, and several small companies that brought new antibiotics to market have gone bankrupt. Governments are experimenting with subscription schemes, under which a health service pays a fixed annual fee for access to a drug regardless of how many doses are used. The aim is to separate a company's income from its sales, so that doctors can use the drug sparingly without ruining the business that made it. Whether such schemes can be funded on a large enough scale is not yet clear.

G
Other approaches are being explored alongside new drugs. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill bacteria, are being tested as a way of treating infections that no antibiotic can cure. Rapid diagnostic tests, which tell a doctor within an hour whether an infection is bacterial and which drug will work, could replace the habit of prescribing a broad-spectrum antibiotic as a precaution. Vaccines reduce the number of infections in the first place and, by doing so, the number of antibiotics prescribed; the vaccine against pneumococcal disease, for instance, has been followed by a fall in resistant cases of that disease. No single measure is likely to be enough. Dr Moravec argues that the realistic goal is not to abolish resistance, which natural selection makes impossible, but to slow it sufficiently for new treatments to keep pace.

items.text:
A
The phrase sharing economy is something of a misnomer. Little of what it describes involves sharing in the sense of giving freely; most of it involves strangers paying to use things they do not own. Economists therefore prefer terms such as the access economy or the platform economy. The underlying idea is simple. A private car spends around ninety-five per cent of its life parked, a spare bedroom may be empty for most of the year, and a power drill is typically used for a few minutes in its entire lifetime. These are examples of idle capacity, assets already paid for that generate no income. If they could be put to work cheaply, both owners and users would gain, and the economy would obtain more service from the same stock of goods. What prevented this in the past was not a lack of willing owners but the cost of arranging each transaction.

B
The economist Ronald Coase argued that such transaction costs, the effort of finding a partner, agreeing terms, checking quality and collecting payment, explain why so many activities are organised inside firms rather than through markets. Digital platforms reduce several of these costs at once. A smartphone shows which drivers are nearby, calculates a price, handles payment and records the trip. Renting a stranger's drill for one afternoon, once absurdly impractical, becomes a transaction taking less than a minute. Platforms do not create the underlying assets; they create the market in which previously unmarketable services can be traded, and they take a commission, commonly between fifteen and thirty per cent, for doing so.

C
Lower search costs do not, however, solve the problem of trust. A stranger who rents a spare room cannot easily judge the cleanliness of a flat, and the owner cannot judge the guest's habits. Economists call this information asymmetry, and George Akerlof's classic study of the used-car market showed that it can destroy a market altogether, as buyers who cannot distinguish good products from bad refuse to pay a fair price for either. Platforms respond with reputation systems in which both sides rate each other. These work surprisingly well, yet they have flaws. On many platforms the great majority of ratings are 4.5 out of five or higher, so a score carries little information. Field experiments have also found that hosts are less likely to accept guests whose names suggest a minority background, which shows that a reputation system can copy human prejudice as well as correct it.

D
A second economic feature is the network effect. A ride-hailing service is more valuable to passengers when it has many drivers, and more attractive to drivers when it has many passengers, so each side of the market draws in the other. Economists call such businesses two-sided markets. Network effects favour early leaders: a platform that reaches critical mass quickly can dominate a city, while a smaller rival struggles to attract either group. To reach that point, many platforms spend heavily on subsidies, charging prices that do not cover their costs and financing the shortfall with investors' money. Consumers enjoy the discounts, but the strategy raises a question that cannot be answered in advance: whether prices will rise once competition has been reduced. Dr Linnea Aldous of the Veldmark School of Economics suggests that the answer depends less on the technology than on how easily users can move between competing platforms.

E
The effects on labour are the most disputed. Platform work offers a way to earn money at times of the worker's choosing, and surveys regularly find that people value this flexibility; for many, the income supplements another job. Yet most platform workers are classified as independent contractors, which usually means no sick pay, holiday pay or minimum wage. Once fuel, insurance and the fall in value of the vehicle are deducted, hourly earnings can be well below the headline figure. There is also a structural problem. When earnings look attractive, more people sign up, and with more drivers sharing a fixed number of passengers, each earns less. Entry therefore continues until the gains from flexibility are almost cancelled out. Courts in different countries have reached opposite verdicts on whether such workers should be treated as employees.

F
Established industries have also been affected. In many cities a taxi licence once cost a large sum and was treated as a valuable asset; when ride-hailing arrived, its market price fell sharply in some places. Incumbents argue that the new entrants avoid rules, such as safety inspections and taxes, that apply to them. Platforms reply that those rules were designed to deal with problems of information and safety that their ratings and tracking now address. Regulators face a genuine dilemma: apply old rules to new businesses, which may suppress useful innovation, or write new ones, which takes time and may leave consumers unprotected in the meantime. Housing shows the difficulty clearly. Short-term rental platforms allow owners to earn more from a spare room, but a study of American cities found that a ten per cent increase in listings was associated with a rise in rents of under one per cent, an effect concentrated in popular neighbourhoods where tourists compete with residents for the same homes.

G
Claims that the sharing economy is good for the environment deserve similar caution. Using an existing car or drill more intensively should reduce the need to manufacture new ones. But cheaper services can lead people to consume more, a phenomenon known as the rebound effect: studies in several cities suggest that ride-hailing has drawn passengers away from buses, trains and walking, increasing the number of vehicles on the road. The most defensible conclusion is that the sharing economy is neither the revolution its advocates promised nor the sham its critics allege. It lowers certain frictions, and what it delivers depends largely on the rules within which it operates.

items.text:
A
In April 1815, the volcano Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted with a force not seen in recorded history. Tens of thousands of people died in the immediate vicinity, but the consequences were not confined to the region. The following year, much of Europe and North America experienced a cold, wet summer in which frosts struck in June and crops rotted in the fields. Grain prices soared, food riots broke out in several countries, and famine and disease followed. The year 1816 became known as the year without a summer. Contemporaries had no idea that the cause lay on the far side of the globe, and it was decades before anyone proposed a link. One famous product of the gloomy weather was a ghost story written by a young woman who was confined indoors beside Lake Geneva.

B
The mechanism is now well understood. Ash, though dramatic, falls out of the atmosphere within weeks and has little effect on climate. What matters is sulphur dioxide. If an eruption is powerful enough to inject this gas into the stratosphere, more than ten kilometres above the surface, it reacts with water to form tiny droplets of sulphuric acid, called aerosols. Above the weather, nothing washes them out, so they can remain for a year or two, reflecting a small fraction of incoming sunlight back to space. The result is a global cooling of perhaps half a degree to one degree Celsius, enough to shorten growing seasons and disrupt monsoon rains. Crucially, the size of an eruption is not a reliable guide to its climatic impact: a modest eruption that delivers a large amount of sulphur high into the stratosphere can cool the planet more than a larger one that does not.

C
Because the aerosols leave a chemical signature, past eruptions can be traced in polar ice. Each year's snowfall compresses into a layer, and by drilling cores from Greenland and Antarctica, scientists can count the layers like tree rings and measure the sulphate they contain. A spike that appears in both polar regions at the same time indicates a large tropical eruption, whose aerosols spread to both hemispheres; a spike in only one suggests an eruption at high latitude. Tree rings provide a second record. Narrow rings, and in cold conditions rings with frost damage, show years of poor growth, and by matching the two records researchers can date events to the nearest year, or sometimes the season. This precision has led to some surprising discoveries.

D
One of them concerns the sixth century. A Byzantine official recorded that in 536 the sun gave light like the moon for a whole year. Chinese records describe summer frost, Irish chronicles refer to failures of bread, and tree rings from Scandinavia to Chile show severe cooling. For decades the cause was unknown. Ice cores eventually revealed a large sulphate deposit dated to early 536, and a later study of ice chemistry concluded that the likely source was an eruption in Iceland. A second eruption followed in 540, so the climate had little chance to recover. Some historians connect this troubled period with famine and with the plague that struck the Byzantine Empire in the early 540s, although the extent of the volcanic contribution remains debated.

E
Not every eruption has been identified so neatly. For years, ice cores showed a huge sulphate signal around 1257, larger than Tambora's, yet no volcano could be matched to it. In 2013 a team of researchers combined radiocarbon dating of charred trees, analysis of volcanic glass and medieval chronicles to show that the culprit was Samalas, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Lombok, whose collapse left a lake-filled caldera. The eruption appears to have been followed by cold, wet summers across Europe, although historians caution that bad weather in medieval records is hard to attribute to a single cause, since poor harvests had many explanations.

F
Eruptions need not be explosive to be harmful. In 1783 the Laki fissure in Iceland spent eight months releasing lava and gases, including large quantities of fluorine and sulphur dioxide. Fluorine poisoned the grazing land, and most of the country's livestock died, followed by a famine that killed roughly a fifth of the population. The haze drifted across Europe, where it was blamed for a sharp rise in deaths in some countries. Some historians go further and argue that the hardship caused by poor harvests in the following years added to the social tensions in France before 1789, although such claims are very difficult to prove.

G
The most contested case is far older. About 74,000 years ago, Toba in Sumatra produced the largest eruption of the last two million years. In the 1990s it was proposed that the resulting volcanic winter reduced the human population to a few thousand individuals. Genetic evidence for such a bottleneck, however, is open to other interpretations, and excavations in India have found that communities making stone tools continued through the eruption layer without an obvious break. Many researchers now think that the effects were serious but regional. The debate matters beyond history. Volcanologists estimate that eruptions on the scale of Tambora occur roughly once or twice in every thousand years, and societies today, with the global trade in grain dependent on a few producing regions, could find that a sudden failure of harvests spreads rapidly from one continent to another.

items.text:
The table shows the average number of hours per week that adults in four age groups spent on four leisure activities in a European country in 2023.

Age 18-29: streaming video 9, social media 7, sport 4, reading 1
Age 30-49: streaming video 7, social media 5, sport 3, reading 2
Age 50-64: streaming video 10, social media 3, sport 3, reading 4
Age 65 and over: streaming video 14, social media 2, sport 2, reading 6

Note: figures are weekly averages per person.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how much time adults in four age groups spent on four leisure activities each week in 2023. Overall, streaming video took up the most time for every group, while the pattern for social media and reading changed sharply with age.

Streaming video was the most popular activity in all four groups, but the figure rose with age from 9 hours among 18 to 29 year olds to 14 hours among people aged 65 and over, apart from a dip to 7 hours in the 30 to 49 group. Social media shows the opposite trend. The youngest group spent 7 hours on it, compared with only 2 hours for the oldest group, a difference of 5 hours.

Reading was the least popular activity for the two younger groups, at 1 and 2 hours, but it became more important with age, reaching 6 hours for the over 65s, which was three times the figure for the 30 to 49 group. Sport was the most stable activity, ranging only between 2 and 4 hours, and it was highest among the youngest adults.

In total, the oldest group had the most leisure time, at 24 hours, while the 30 to 49 group had the least, at 17 hours.

items.q: Some people believe that public money should be spent on preserving old buildings, while others think it would be better spent on new housing and public facilities. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
Governments have limited budgets, and deciding between the preservation of historic buildings and the construction of new housing is a difficult choice. While both sides have merit, I believe that a balanced approach is best, with priority given to urgent social needs.

Those who favour preservation argue that old buildings are a link with the past. They give a town its character, teach younger generations about their history, and attract tourists, who spend money in local shops and hotels. Once a historic building has been demolished, it cannot be replaced, so supporters claim that public money is the only way to protect it, since private owners often cannot afford the repairs.

On the other hand, many cities face a serious shortage of affordable homes, and young families are being pushed out by rising rents. Spending large sums to restore a building that few people visit may seem hard to justify when others have nowhere decent to live. New schools, clinics and public transport also improve daily life for far more people than a museum or an old church can.

In my opinion, the two aims are not always in competition. Many old buildings can be converted into apartments, libraries or community centres, which saves them from decay while serving modern needs. Governments should protect only those buildings that have real historical or architectural value, and should encourage private companies to share the cost through tax benefits. Everything else should be judged by how much it helps ordinary citizens.

In conclusion, preserving heritage is worthwhile, but housing and public services must come first when money is short. A wise policy combines the two wherever possible.

items.vi: Mẫu trả lời: thích đọc tiểu thuyết và bài báo khoa học, đọc nửa tiếng mỗi tối để thư giãn.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a journey that you remember well. You should say: where you went, how you travelled, who you went with, and explain why you remember this journey so well.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a train journey that I took with my cousin two summers ago, from our home city to a small town in the mountains. We went to visit our grandparents, whom we had not seen for almost a year. The trip took about six hours, and we travelled by train because my cousin is afraid of flying and the roads are very winding. The first part was quite ordinary, but after a few hours the train began to climb into the mountains, and the view was beautiful, with green valleys, waterfalls and tiny villages. We talked, played cards and shared the sandwiches that my mother had packed. At one point the train stopped for an hour because of a landslide on the track, and we became friendly with a family sitting opposite, who offered us fruit. I remember this journey so well because it was the first time that I travelled without my parents, and I felt very independent. It also reminded me that the journey itself can be as enjoyable as the destination, and I would love to repeat it one day.
items.vi: Mẫu Part 2: kể về chuyến tàu đến vùng núi cùng người anh họ và lý do nhớ mãi.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss more abstract questions related to the Part 2 topic.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề phần 2.

items.q: Why do you think more people travel abroad today than in the past?
items.sample: I think there are several reasons. Flights have become cheaper, and the internet makes it much easier to book tickets and hotels. Also, people earn more than before, and many see travel as a way to learn about other cultures, so it has become part of normal life.
items.vi: Mẫu trả lời: vé máy bay rẻ hơn, đặt chỗ dễ hơn nhờ internet, thu nhập cao hơn và mong muốn tìm hiểu văn hóa khác.

items.q: What problems can a large number of tourists cause for a place?
items.sample: Too many tourists can make popular places crowded and noisy, and local residents may find that prices of housing and food rise. In addition, heavy traffic and rubbish can damage the environment, so some cities have started to limit the number of visitors.
items.vi: Mẫu trả lời: quá nhiều du khách gây đông đúc, tăng giá nhà và thức ăn, gây hại môi trường nên một số thành phố giới hạn số khách.

items.q: Do you think travelling by train will become more popular in the future?
items.sample: I believe it will, mainly because people are more worried about the environment, and trains produce much less pollution than planes. If governments build faster lines and keep tickets affordable, many travellers will choose the train for short and medium distances in the future.
items.vi: Mẫu trả lời: tàu hỏa sẽ phổ biến hơn vì thân thiện môi trường hơn máy bay nếu tuyến nhanh và vé rẻ.

parts.instr: Complete the form. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
parts.instrVi: Hoàn thành mẫu đăng ký. Viết MỘT TỪ và/hoặc MỘT SỐ cho mỗi câu trả lời.

audio.t: Good morning, Fernwood Arts Centre. How can I help?
Hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your weekend bookbinding workshops, if there are any left.
Certainly. Can I take your surname, please?
It's Tavares. That's T-A-V-A-R-E-S.
Thank you, Mr. Tavares. And a contact number?
Yes, it's 07700 3814. Sorry, I mean 4821. I always mix up the last four digits.

4821. Got it. Now, we're running two workshops this autumn. One is Coptic binding, where the pages are sewn together with a chain stitch along the spine. The other is Japanese stab binding, which is a little simpler and produces a flat, decorative edge.
I've seen photos of the Japanese style, and I like the look of it. I'll take that one.
Japanese stab binding, then. It runs on two Saturdays. The first is the eleventh of October, but I'm afraid that one is full. The second is the eighteenth, and there are still three places.
The eighteenth is fine. What time does it start?
Doors open at half past nine for registration, but the class itself starts at ten and finishes at four.
And how much is it?
It's sixty-five dollars for the tuition. Materials cost another twenty, so eighty-five altogether, and that includes your paper, thread and a set of tools that you can keep.
That sounds reasonable. Do I need to bring anything?
Not much. We supply everything, but I'd suggest an apron, because the glue can be messy. Some people bring their own scissors, but you really don't need to.
Where do I go when I arrive? Is it the main hall?
No, the main hall is used for the pottery fair that weekend. You'll be in the Cedar Studio, on the first floor. The Elm Studio next to it is for the painting class.
And is there anywhere to get lunch?
There's a cafe across the courtyard that sells sandwiches and soup. Most people eat there, but you're welcome to bring a packed lunch.
Great. One last thing. Where's the best place to park?
Our own car park is closed for repairs, so use the one on Mill Street, about five minutes' walk away. Don't use the one on Quay Road, because that's for residents only.
Thank you. That's very helpful.
You're welcome. I'll send a confirmation by email. We look forward to seeing you.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a new late-night opening service at a library and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về dịch vụ mở cửa buổi tối mới của một thư viện và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the launch of Late Library at Ashgrove Central Library. I'm Priya Nandakumar, the head of community services, and I'd like to explain how this new service came about and what you can expect from it.

For many years the library closed at six o'clock on weekdays. A survey of residents carried out two years ago found that the biggest complaint was not a lack of books or computers, but the opening hours. Nearly half the people who answered said they finished work too late to visit. We had expected that students would be the main group asking for longer hours, but they came second.

So, from this month, the library will stay open until ten o'clock on Wednesdays and Thursdays. This is a six-month trial, not a permanent change. If enough people use the service, the council will decide whether to extend it to other evenings. We have to be realistic, because the extra staff will cost about forty thousand dollars for the trial period, and that money came from a one-off grant.

Not every part of the building will stay open. The ground floor and the first floor will be available, which includes the lending section, the computer suite and the reading room. The second floor, where the local history archive is kept, closes at six as usual, because we don't have enough trained staff to supervise the rare documents after that time.

Late Library is not simply a longer day. Each Wednesday evening we're running a free activity at seven o'clock. Next week it's a talk by a retired ship's engineer, and after that there is a writing group and a beginners' course in family history research. On Thursdays, by contrast, we keep the building quiet, and the reading room is reserved for silent study, since several students told us they needed a calm place to revise for exams.

A few practical points. Entry after six o'clock is through the side door on Harbour Street, not the main entrance, which is locked at six. You'll need to show your library card to the security officer, and if you haven't got one, you can register at the desk in about five minutes. Visitors under sixteen must be accompanied by an adult after seven o'clock.

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor about a project on old maps and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư về dự án bản đồ cổ và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. I've read your project outline on early printed maps. Where are you up to?
Thanks, Dr. Whitcombe. We've chosen to compare three maps of the same coastline, made in the sixteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, to see how the accuracy changed.
We originally wanted to include a fourth map from the fifteenth century, but we couldn't find a good-quality image of it.
I'd leave it out in any case. Three maps give you enough to compare, and four would make the report far too long. What's your measure of accuracy?
We planned to overlay each map on a modern satellite image and measure how far the main harbors are from their true positions.

That's sensible, but be careful. A map isn't just a failed attempt at a satellite photograph. Mapmakers had different purposes. A sea chart was meant to help a captain find a port, and the shape of a distant inland region mattered much less to him.
So we should explain the purpose of each map before we judge it.
Exactly. Put that in your introduction, with a paragraph on who paid for each map and who was expected to use it.
I hadn't thought about who paid. The earliest one was commissioned by a merchant company, wasn't it, Marcus?
Yes. So it probably exaggerated the size of the harbors that were useful for trade.
Quite possibly. That's the kind of argument that will lift your mark. Now, the method. How will you handle the measurements?
We were going to do them by hand with a ruler and then calculate the average error.

I'd advise against it. Use the free mapping software in the library computer suite. It lets you place points on the old map and calculates the distortion automatically. You'll save several days, and it reduces human error.
We didn't know the library had that. Do we need training?
There's a one-hour workshop every Tuesday. You book through the library website.
What about the sources for the history? We've mostly used one textbook.
That's your weak point. One textbook gives you one opinion. I'd like to see at least two journal articles, and ideally one that disagrees with the textbook.
There's a recent article arguing that the second map was copied from a Portuguese original, while the textbook claims it was drawn from fresh surveys.
Then you have a ready-made debate. Use it, but don't simply say who you think is right. Weigh the evidence on each side.
When is the deadline?
The draft is due on the twelfth of March, and the final version two weeks later. I'll give feedback on the draft within a week, but I won't read anything that's late.
Should we write the report together or separately?
Divide it. Leila, you take the history of the maps, and Marcus, you take the measurements. Then write the conclusion together, because that is where your two halves must agree.
And the presentation? Do we need slides?
A poster is better in this case, because people can see the overlays side by side. But keep the text short. I would rather see a clear image than a paragraph.
That makes sense. Thank you, Dr. Whitcombe.
