audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about hydrothermal vents, which are among the strangest habitats on Earth, and about what they have taught us about the limits of life.

Vents were discovered in 1977 by a team of geologists who were actually looking for warm water along an undersea mountain range. They lowered a camera to a depth of about two thousand five hundred meters and found, to their astonishment, dense colonies of giant tube worms and clams in total darkness. Until then, biologists had assumed that all ecosystems depended on sunlight.

The vents form along mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates are moving apart. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the crust, is heated by magma to temperatures above 350 degrees Celsius, and then rises again carrying dissolved minerals. When this hot fluid meets the near-freezing water of the deep ocean, the minerals precipitate and form chimneys. The dark fluid gives rise to the name black smokers, because the particles are rich in iron sulfide.

The base of the food web is not a plant but a microbe. Bacteria obtain energy from hydrogen sulfide in the fluid, a process called chemosynthesis. The giant tube worms, which can grow to over two meters, have no mouth and no stomach as adults. Instead, they house bacteria inside a special organ called the trophosome. The worm supplies the bacteria with the chemicals they need, and in return it receives nutrients.

Vent communities are remarkably rich. A single chimney may support dozens of species, among them shrimp, crabs, snails and fish. The animals are adapted to extreme conditions. Some shrimp lack functional eyes but have a sensor on their backs that detects the faint glow of the hot rock.

Vents are also short-lived by geological standards. A chimney may collapse after a few decades, or the flow of fluid may stop altogether, and the community must then be replaced by larvae that drift in from other vents, sometimes over distances of several hundred kilometers. Scientists have observed colonies re-establishing within about two years after a volcanic eruption wiped out an entire field.

In recent years vents have attracted attention for two other reasons. First, some scientists suspect that life on Earth may have begun in a similar setting, where chemical energy was abundant and the surface was shielded from harsh radiation and meteorite impacts. Second, the mineral deposits around vents contain copper, zinc and gold, and companies have proposed mining them. Researchers warn that because the communities are so isolated, removing even a single chimney could destroy species that live nowhere else, and recovery could take decades.

Finally, the same research has changed the search for life beyond our planet. Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn are covered by ice, but beneath it there may be oceans in contact with hot rock. If chemosynthesis works in the dark on Earth, it might work there. That is why many space agencies now study the deep ocean as a rehearsal for exploring other worlds.

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about hydrothermal vents, which are among the strangest habitats on Earth, and about what they have taught us about the limits of life.

Vents were discovered in 1977 by a team of geologists who were actually looking for warm water along an undersea mountain range. They lowered a camera to a depth of about two thousand five hundred meters and found, to their astonishment, dense colonies of giant tube worms and clams in total darkness. Until then, biologists had assumed that all ecosystems depended on sunlight.

The vents form along mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates are moving apart. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the crust, is heated by magma to temperatures above 350 degrees Celsius, and then rises again carrying dissolved minerals. When this hot fluid meets the near-freezing water of the deep ocean, the minerals precipitate and form chimneys. The dark fluid gives rise to the name black smokers, because the particles are rich in iron sulfide.

The base of the food web is not a plant but a microbe. Bacteria obtain energy from hydrogen sulfide in the fluid, a process called chemosynthesis. The giant tube worms, which can grow to over two meters, have no mouth and no stomach as adults. Instead, they house bacteria inside a special organ called the trophosome. The worm supplies the bacteria with the chemicals they need, and in return it receives nutrients.

Vent communities are remarkably rich. A single chimney may support dozens of species, among them shrimp, crabs, snails and fish. The animals are adapted to extreme conditions. Some shrimp lack functional eyes but have a sensor on their backs that detects the faint glow of the hot rock.

Vents are also short-lived by geological standards. A chimney may collapse after a few decades, or the flow of fluid may stop altogether, and the community must then be replaced by larvae that drift in from other vents, sometimes over distances of several hundred kilometers. Scientists have observed colonies re-establishing within about two years after a volcanic eruption wiped out an entire field.

In recent years vents have attracted attention for two other reasons. First, some scientists suspect that life on Earth may have begun in a similar setting, where chemical energy was abundant and the surface was shielded from harsh radiation and meteorite impacts. Second, the mineral deposits around vents contain copper, zinc and gold, and companies have proposed mining them. Researchers warn that because the communities are so isolated, removing even a single chimney could destroy species that live nowhere else, and recovery could take decades.

Finally, the same research has changed the search for life beyond our planet. Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn are covered by ice, but beneath it there may be oceans in contact with hot rock. If chemosynthesis works in the dark on Earth, it might work there. That is why many space agencies now study the deep ocean as a rehearsal for exploring other worlds.

items.text:
A
For much of the twentieth century, evolutionary biology was dominated by an image of nature as a perpetual contest. Darwin's phrase, the struggle for existence, was often compressed into a slogan about competition in which every individual strives only to leave more offspring than its rivals. That picture sits uneasily with the facts of the living world. Ants build cities, wolves hunt in packs, and bacteria release chemicals that pay off only when millions of cells do the same. If selection favors the selfish, why is cooperation so widespread? The puzzle is sharpest when cooperation is costly: an animal that shares food or gives a warning call sacrifices something for the benefit of another, and a gene for such generosity ought, on the face of it, to disappear within a few generations.

B
The first influential answer came from the biologist Edmund Rawlings in the 1960s. He pointed out that a gene can spread not only by helping its bearer reproduce but also by helping relatives, who are likely to carry copies of the same gene. A parent that risks its life for its young, or a worker bee that never breeds but tends its sisters, can be understood as promoting its own genes by proxy. Rawlings proposed that such helping behavior evolves when the benefit to the recipient, multiplied by the degree of relatedness, exceeds the cost to the helper. Kin selection explained an enormous range of behavior, and in social insects it accounts for the extreme sterility of workers. Yet it could not explain cooperation between unrelated individuals, which is common in primates, fish and, above all, humans.

C
A second mechanism, reciprocity, was explored by the theorist Marta Coelho and tested in the 1980s by the political scientist Henrik Dahl, who invited experts to submit strategies for a repeated game known as the prisoner's dilemma. In a single round, the rational choice is to betray one's partner; over many rounds, however, mutual betrayal leaves both players worse off than steady cooperation. The winning strategy, submitted by a mathematician, was strikingly simple. It cooperated on the first move and thereafter copied whatever the other player had done previously. Dahl noted that successful strategies shared several traits: they were never the first to betray, they responded to betrayal promptly, they forgave quickly, and they were easy for others to understand. Reciprocity works, in other words, only when partners are likely to meet again and can recognize one another.

D
Humans, however, cooperate with strangers they will never meet again, a feat that neither kinship nor simple reciprocity can fully explain. Here, researchers have turned to reputation. In experiments, people who give generously to others are later rewarded by third parties who have only heard about their conduct. Gossip, in this view, is not a trivial vice but a technology for monitoring behavior, and language may have evolved partly because it let groups share information about who could be trusted. The effect is powerful but fragile. It depends on information being reasonably accurate, and it breaks down in large anonymous populations unless institutions such as courts, ratings and public records take over the work that gossip once did.

E
A further line of research concerns punishment. In a well-known set of laboratory games devised by the economist Ingrid Solberg, players could contribute to a common pot, which was then multiplied and shared equally. Without sanctions, contributions collapsed as players realized they could free-ride on others. When participants were allowed to pay a small fee to fine those who contributed little, cooperation rebounded and stayed high. Strikingly, many people were willing to punish even when they gained nothing personally, and societies differ markedly in how far this willingness extends. In some places punishment is applied evenly; in others, free-riders retaliate against the people who punish them, and cooperation fails to recover. The finding suggests that the norms surrounding sanctions matter as much as the sanctions themselves.

F
Some theorists have gone further and proposed that selection can operate at the level of groups. Individuals who cooperate lose out within their own group to selfish neighbors, yet groups with many cooperators outcompete groups with few. The idea was dismissed for decades as naive, but in recent years it has been revived in a more rigorous form, particularly to account for human history, in which warfare and competition between communities were frequent. Critics respond that the same results can be obtained by counting the effects on individuals, and that the debate is largely one of bookkeeping rather than of fact. What most researchers now accept is that no single mechanism suffices. Cooperation has arisen many times, and it rests on kinship in the ant colony, reciprocity in the vampire bat, reputation in the human village and, in all likelihood, a blend of these in the modern city.

items.text:
A
Every large city is, among other things, a machine for moving water. Rain that once soaked into soil and fed streams is intercepted by roofs and roads, and gathered into pipes that carry it away as quickly as possible; meanwhile, other pipes bring in drinking water from reservoirs that may lie hundreds of kilometers away. For a century and a half, this arrangement was regarded as one of the triumphs of modern engineering, and with good reason. It ended the epidemics of cholera and typhoid that had once swept through crowded districts. But the system was designed for a climate and a population that no longer exist, and many cities now face the dual problem of too little water in some months and too much in others.

B
The conventional approach, sometimes called gray infrastructure, relies on concrete and steel: reservoirs, culverts, treatment plants and enormous storm sewers. Its virtue is predictability, since a sewer of a given diameter can be relied on to carry a known volume. Its weakness is rigidity. Pipes laid in the nineteenth century were sized for the rainfall of that time, and increasingly intense storms overwhelm them, forcing combined sewers to discharge a mixture of rainwater and sewage into rivers. Enlarging the pipes is possible but ruinously expensive, because it means digging up streets that are already crowded with cables, tunnels and foundations. The city of Marlow Bay, for example, estimated that eliminating overflows entirely by tunneling would cost more than its municipal budget for ten years.

C
A different philosophy has therefore gained ground, often described by the phrase "sponge city". Instead of removing rain as waste, designers try to slow it, store it and let it soak back into the ground close to where it fell. The tools are modest in appearance: roofs planted with vegetation, pavements that let water pass through, shallow basins called bioswales along roadsides, and parks deliberately designed to flood during storms and drain afterward. Individually, each measure absorbs only a small amount. Collectively, a network of them can reduce peak flows into sewers by a third or more, and their effect is cumulative rather than all-or-nothing, which means they can be added piece by piece as budgets allow.

D
Advocates also point to benefits that have little to do with drainage. Vegetation cools streets in summer, filters pollutants from runoff and provides habitat, while pleasant green spaces tend to raise the value of neighboring property. Skeptics reply that such additional benefits are hard to measure and are sometimes used to inflate the case for projects that do not, in fact, solve the flooding problem. A review of forty schemes in northern Europe found that the green measures performed well in moderate storms but made little difference in the most extreme events, which are precisely the ones that cause the greatest damage. The authors concluded that green and gray approaches are complementary rather than competing: the former handles frequent, small rainfall, the latter the rare catastrophe.

E
Reuse is the other half of the story. Cities in arid regions have long recognized that wastewater is a resource rather than a nuisance. In the desert port of Qasr Almina, treated sewage is purified to a standard that exceeds that of many bottled waters and is then injected into the aquifer, where natural filtration continues the work and the water mingles with the groundwater from which the city draws its supply. The technology is dependable; the obstacle is psychological. Surveys consistently show that residents accept recycled water for irrigation and industry, but balk at the idea of drinking it, an attitude researchers call the "yuck factor". Utilities that have succeeded in overcoming it have generally done so through patient education, public tours of the plants and, in one notable case, a campaign in which a popular brewery made beer from the purified water.

F
Pricing is a further lever, and one that is politically delicate. Water is typically sold at a price far below its true cost of collection, treatment and delivery, because it is regarded as a basic right. Low prices, however, give households little reason to repair leaking taps or install efficient appliances, and the leaks in the pipe network itself can be enormous; in some older cities, a third of the treated water never reaches a customer. Tiered tariffs, in which the first quantity of water needed for essential uses is cheap and additional consumption becomes progressively more expensive, are one attempt to reconcile fairness with conservation. Their critics point out that large families, who may use more water through no fault of their own, can be penalized unless the tiers are adjusted for household size.

G
Looking ahead, the greatest challenge may be less technical than institutional. Water in a typical city is managed by separate agencies responsible for drinking supply, sewage, storm drainage and parks, each with its own budget and priorities. A bioswale that benefits the sewer department may be built on land belonging to the parks department and maintained by no one. The cities that have made the most progress have usually created a single authority, or at least a shared plan, that treats the urban water cycle as one system. The lesson is a humbling one for engineers: the hardest pipes to rearrange are the ones that connect organizations rather than buildings.

items.text:
A
Beneath the sea lies the largest museum in the world, though it has no walls, no guards and no catalog. Estimates suggest that millions of wrecks lie scattered across the seabed, from dugout canoes to steamships. To the archaeologist, a wreck has a quality that few land sites can offer: it is a closed assemblage, a sealed moment. A house is occupied for centuries, rebuilt, looted and abandoned, so that its layers blur together. A ship that founders in a storm carries everything on board down with it at a single instant, so that the cargo, the tools, the crew's belongings and the food they ate are all tied to the same day.

B
Reaching that moment is difficult. Early underwater excavation was conducted by divers in heavy helmets, and its results were frequently poor, since the work was done quickly and recorded badly. The change came in the middle of the twentieth century, when the invention of the aqualung allowed archaeologists to dive for themselves rather than rely on professional salvors. A series of excavations of Bronze Age wrecks off the Mediterranean coast during the 1960s and 1970s demonstrated that the standards of land archaeology could be applied underwater. Grids were laid across the site, every object was mapped before it was lifted, and divers were trained as archaeologists rather than the reverse.

C
Conditions on the seabed determine what survives. In warm, shallow water, wooden hulls are quickly consumed by shipworms, mollusks that bore through timber, leaving only the heavy cargo and ballast stones lying in a mound. In the cold, brackish waters of the Baltic Sea, where shipworms cannot live because the salt content is too low, wrecks have lasted astonishingly well. Masts have been found standing upright, and one vessel lost more than three centuries ago was raised with its carved decoration still visible. Burial in silt can help a wreck by shutting out oxygen, while strong currents and fishing nets can scatter and destroy it. Archaeologists therefore consider the environment of a site before deciding whether to excavate at all.

D
What can be learned goes well beyond the vessel itself. A cargo is evidence of trade: the origin of pottery jars can be traced to particular workshops through the chemistry of the clay, revealing routes and partnerships that no written record mentions. The personal possessions of the crew show who was aboard. On one merchant vessel lost in the sixteen hundreds, the remains of cooking pots, gaming pieces and a carved comb showed that the crew came from at least three different countries, a detail that the ship's official papers had omitted. Even the repairs to a hull can be informative, because the style of carpentry often indicates where and when the work was done, and therefore the route the ship had followed.

E
Once an object has lain in the sea for centuries, bringing it up can destroy it. Waterlogged wood is held together by water; if it dries out, it shrinks and cracks. Iron objects are coated in concretions, hard crusts of rust and sand, which can hide the shape of what is inside and which release salts that corrode the metal once exposed to air. Conservation is therefore slow and costly. A single cannon may spend several years in tanks of fresh water while the salts are drawn out, and a large hull may need a decade of treatment with preserving chemicals. Because the cost of conservation can exceed the cost of the excavation many times over, some archaeologists now argue that the best option for many wrecks is to leave them where they lie.

F
That argument is reinforced by the problem of looting. Improved diving equipment and cheap sonar have placed even deep wrecks within reach of treasure hunters, who sell their finds to private collectors and in the process destroy the context that gives objects their meaning. A coin removed without record tells us little; the same coin found in a documented position beside a dated chest tells us a great deal. An international convention has gradually extended protection, and declares that underwater cultural heritage should not be commercially exploited. Yet enforcing such rules in the open ocean, far from any national jurisdiction, is extremely hard, and some countries have declined to sign the agreement.

G
New technology offers some hope. Autonomous underwater vehicles can survey large areas of seabed and produce detailed maps without a diver in the water. Photogrammetry, in which thousands of overlapping photographs are combined by software, creates three-dimensional models accurate to within a few millimeters, so that a wreck can be studied in detail without lifting a single object. Some museums now display these digital models alongside, or even instead of, the artifacts. Enthusiasts claim that the technique will allow the public to visit wrecks that remain on the seabed; skeptics reply that a model, however precise, cannot tell us what is hidden inside a lump of concretion. Probably both are right, and the future of the field lies in careful selection: excavating only those wrecks that are threatened, and leaving the rest for generations with better tools.

parts.instr: Writing Task 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Writing Task 1. Nên dành khoảng 20 phút. Viết ít nhất 150 từ.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of electricity generated from five sources in the country of Norland in 1995, 2005 and 2015.

Coal: 48 (1995), 36 (2005), 19 (2015)
Natural gas: 22 (1995), 30 (2005), 31 (2015)
Nuclear power: 20 (1995), 17 (2005), 12 (2015)
Hydroelectric power: 8 (1995), 9 (2005), 11 (2015)
Wind and solar power: 2 (1995), 8 (2005), 27 (2015)
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the share of electricity that Norland produced from five different sources in 1995, 2005 and 2015. Overall, the country moved away from coal and nuclear power and towards natural gas and, above all, wind and solar power, which showed the most dramatic change.

In 1995, coal was by far the leading source, supplying 48 percent of electricity, more than twice the share of natural gas at 22 percent. Nuclear power came third with 20 percent, while hydroelectric power and wind and solar power together contributed only 10 percent.

Over the following two decades, coal declined steadily to 36 percent in 2005 and then to just 19 percent in 2015. Nuclear power also fell, although more gradually, reaching 12 percent by the end of the period. By contrast, natural gas rose to 30 percent and then edged up to 31 percent, making it the largest source in 2015. Hydroelectric power grew slightly from 8 to 11 percent.

The most striking trend was the rise of wind and solar power. Starting at a mere 2 percent, it quadrupled to 8 percent in 2005 and then more than trebled to 27 percent in 2015, overtaking coal and nuclear power and becoming the second most important source.
items.vi: Bài mẫu mở đầu bằng cái nhìn tổng quát (overall: than và hạt nhân giảm, khí đốt và gió, mặt trời tăng), rồi so sánh số liệu từng năm và nhấn mạnh thay đổi lớn nhất (gió và mặt trời từ 2 lên 27 phần trăm).

parts.instr: Writing Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Writing Task 2. Nên dành khoảng 40 phút. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people think that the main purpose of a university education is to prepare students for employment. Others believe that universities should pursue knowledge for its own sake, whether or not it has a practical use. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
Universities have always served more than one purpose. Some people believe that their main task is to prepare young people for a career, while others argue that they should pursue knowledge for its own sake. In my opinion, both aims are legitimate, but the pursuit of knowledge should remain the foundation of higher education.

Those who favor employment-focused degrees make a reasonable point. Students and their families invest large sums of money and several years of effort, and they naturally expect a good job in return. Courses that include work placements, practical projects and training in current technology can make graduates more confident and more useful to employers. Moreover, a country that trains enough engineers, nurses and teachers benefits as a whole, so it is understandable that governments encourage universities to respond to the needs of the economy.

However, a narrow focus on employment has serious drawbacks. Labor markets change quickly, and a skill that is in demand today may be obsolete in ten years. A graduate who has learned how to think critically, evaluate evidence and communicate clearly is far better prepared for such change than one who has simply memorized a particular technique. In addition, much of the most valuable work done at universities, from basic science to the study of history and philosophy, has no immediate commercial purpose. Research into the structure of atoms or the grammar of ancient languages once seemed useless, yet it has often led to discoveries that nobody predicted.

For these reasons, I believe that universities should treat knowledge as their central mission while helping students to find work through careers advice, internships and links with industry. In conclusion, the two purposes are not rivals. A university that teaches people to think deeply will, in the long run, also produce graduates who are employable.
items.vi: Bài mẫu thảo luận cả hai quan điểm (đại học chuẩn bị nghề nghiệp và đại học theo đuổi tri thức), nêu ý kiến riêng ủng hộ tri thức là nền tảng nhưng vẫn hỗ trợ việc làm, rồi kết luận hai mục đích không đối nghịch.

items.q: Let's talk about reading. Do you enjoy reading in your free time?
items.sample: Yes, I do. I usually read for about an hour before bed because it helps me relax, and I mostly enjoy detective novels and books about history.
items.vi: Trả lời có/không rồi nêu thói quen đọc, thể loại yêu thích và lý do.

items.q: Let's talk about mornings. Are you a morning person?
items.sample: Not really. I usually find it hard to get out of bed in the morning, because I tend to stay up late studying, but I feel much more awake after a cup of tea.
items.vi: Nêu bạn có phải người của buổi sáng không, kèm thói quen và lý do cụ thể.

items.q: Let's talk about the weather. What kind of weather do you like best?
items.sample: I like mild, sunny weather best, because I can go outside and walk or cycle without feeling too hot. I don't like heavy rain because it spoils my plans.
items.vi: Nêu loại thời tiết yêu thích và giải thích vì sao thích hoặc không thích.

items.q: Let's talk about transport. How do you usually travel around your town?
items.sample: I usually take the bus, because it is cheap and there is a stop near my house. When the weather is good, I sometimes walk if the distance is short.
items.vi: Nêu phương tiện thường dùng, lý do và một lựa chọn thay thế.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a book or film that changed the way you think about something. You should say: what it was, when you read or watched it, what it was about, and explain how it changed your thinking.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about a book that changed the way I think about food. It is a non-fiction book about how ordinary vegetables are grown and transported around the world, and I read it two years ago, during the summer holidays, when I had plenty of free time.

The book follows a single tomato from a small farm to a supermarket shelf. The author describes the work of the farmers, the long journeys by truck and ship, and the large amount of food that is thrown away before it is ever eaten. I picked it up because a friend recommended it, and I expected it to be rather dull, but I could not put it down.

It changed my thinking in several ways. Before I read it, I never considered where my meals came from, and I wasted food without feeling guilty. Now I plan what I buy, I try to choose local products, and I think much more carefully about what I throw away. I have also started to cook more at home.

Most importantly, the book taught me that small daily choices can have a real effect, and I often talk about it with my family.
items.vi: Bài mẫu kể về cuốn sách thay đổi cách nghĩ về thực phẩm: nêu tên sách, thời điểm đọc, nội dung và sự thay đổi trong suy nghĩ lẫn hành động.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the more abstract questions related to the topic in Part 2.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề Phần 2.

items.q: Why do some people prefer stories on film to stories in books?
items.sample: I think the main reason is that film is easier and faster, because people can sit back and relax. They can watch without making an effort, and the pictures and music create strong emotions quickly. Reading demands more concentration, so some people feel that it takes too long.
items.vi: Nêu lý do chính: phim dễ xem, nhanh, cảm xúc mạnh, trong khi sách đòi hỏi tập trung và thời gian.

items.q: Do you think fiction can teach people as much as factual writing?
items.sample: In some ways, yes. I think fiction can teach us about emotions and about how other people live, because we imagine ourselves in their position. However, factual writing is better for exact information, so I believe the two kinds of writing teach different things.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm cân bằng: tiểu thuyết dạy về cảm xúc và đời sống, văn bản thực tế dạy thông tin chính xác.

items.q: How might the way people consume stories change over the next few decades?
items.sample: I think technology will make stories more personal. People might watch films that change according to their choices, or listen to books read by artificial voices while they travel. However, I believe that many people will still enjoy a printed book.
items.vi: Dự đoán tương lai: công nghệ làm câu chuyện cá nhân hóa, nhưng sách in vẫn có người ưa chuộng.

audio.t: Harbourside Arts Centre, good afternoon. How can I help you?
Hello. I saw your autumn brochure and I am interested in the printmaking course for beginners.
Certainly. Could I take your name first?
Yes, it is Daniel Penhallow. That is P-E-N-H-A-L-L-O-W.

Thank you, Mr Penhallow. The course is called Introduction to Printmaking. It was due to start on the seventh of October, but I am afraid the studio is being repainted, so the first class is now on Tuesday the fourteenth.
That is fine. What time do the classes begin?
Seven o'clock in the evening, and they finish at half past nine. Some people think that is late, but the studio is only open to us after the pottery group has left.
No problem at all. How long does the course last?
Eight weeks, with no class in the middle week because of the holiday. So the final session is in early December.
And what is the fee?
Normally it is two hundred and ten dollars. However, if you are a student or over sixty-five, there is a concession price of one hundred and eighty-five dollars.
I am retired, so I think I qualify. I am sixty-eight.
Then it is one hundred and eighty-five. Paper, inks and the printing press are all included, but you should bring an old shirt to protect your clothes, because the inks stain badly.
Good idea. Where exactly is the class held?
In the print studio on the second floor. There is a lift if you need it. Parking at the centre is limited, so most people use the Weaver Street car park, which is only a two-minute walk away.
Weaver Street, I know it. How do I book?
I can reserve a place now and send you a confirmation by email. Your booking reference is PR4417. Please quote it when you pay, and payment must be made within ten days.
Lovely. Thank you for your help.
You are welcome. We look forward to seeing you.

Hello. I saw your autumn brochure and I am interested in the printmaking course for beginners.
Certainly. Could I take your name first?
Yes, it is Daniel Penhallow. That is P-E-N-H-A-L-L-O-W.

Thank you, Mr Penhallow. The course is called Introduction to Printmaking. It was due to start on the seventh of October, but I am afraid the studio is being repainted, so the first class is now on Tuesday the fourteenth.
That is fine. What time do the classes begin?
Seven o'clock in the evening, and they finish at half past nine. Some people think that is late, but the studio is only open to us after the pottery group has left.
No problem at all. How long does the course last?
Eight weeks, with no class in the middle week because of the holiday. So the final session is in early December.
And what is the fee?
Normally it is two hundred and ten dollars. However, if you are a student or over sixty-five, there is a concession price of one hundred and eighty-five dollars.
I am retired, so I think I qualify. I am sixty-eight.
Then it is one hundred and eighty-five. Paper, inks and the printing press are all included, but you should bring an old shirt to protect your clothes, because the inks stain badly.
Good idea. Where exactly is the class held?
In the print studio on the second floor. There is a lift if you need it. Parking at the centre is limited, so most people use the Weaver Street car park, which is only a two-minute walk away.
Weaver Street, I know it. How do I book?
I can reserve a place now and send you a confirmation by email. Your booking reference is PR4417. Please quote it when you pay, and payment must be made within ten days.
Lovely. Thank you for your help.
You are welcome. We look forward to seeing you.

audio.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Calder Marsh Nature Reserve. I am the head warden, and over the next few minutes I will explain how the reserve came to exist and how you can enjoy it without disturbing the wildlife.

Many visitors are surprised to learn that this peaceful landscape is only fifteen years old. Until 1998 the whole area was a sand and gravel quarry. When the company left, it wanted to turn the pits into a landfill site, but local residents and fishing clubs objected, and the plan was withdrawn. The land then stood empty for almost a decade, slowly filling with rainwater.

The restoration was paid for mostly by the regional water company. It had been required to create new wetland to make up for marshes lost when a reservoir was built further north, and Calder was the ideal site. The county council contributed a smaller amount, and a university provided scientists to survey the work, but no private donations were involved at that stage.

The first job was to plant reeds across the shallow pools. People often assume they were planted to attract birds, and they do, but the main purpose was to filter fertilizer from the water that runs off the neighboring farmland. Reeds also hold the banks together, although that was a bonus rather than the plan.

The results have been better than anyone predicted. We expected around eighty bird species in the first five years, but last year observers recorded one hundred and twelve. That is still well short of the one hundred and fifty found at the coastal reserve, which has a much wider range of habitats.

Our most famous resident is the bittern, a shy, brown heron that hides in the reeds and is far more often heard than seen. The best chance of spotting one is at dawn in late winter, when the males start to call and the reeds are at their lowest. Summer evenings are lovely, but the reeds are tall then and the birds stay hidden.

A word about the paths. The boardwalk forms two loops. The eastern loop runs close to the main nesting islands, so it is closed from March to July every year. The northern loop and the dyke path stay open all year. Dogs are welcome, but only on the dyke path and only on a lead, because ground-nesting birds are easily frightened.

The reserve depends heavily on volunteers. On Wednesdays, the work party clears young willow trees from the pools. If we left them alone, the water would gradually dry out and the marsh would turn into woodland. We also need people to count birds, but that is done on Sundays, and school visits are led by our education staff.

There is some news for this summer. The cafe is not changing, and neither are our opening hours, but we have just completed a new bird hide with a gentle ramp and wide windows at wheelchair height. It overlooks the largest pool and is already one of the most popular places on the reserve.

If you would like to volunteer, please fill in a form at the information desk or on our website. We do not take applications by telephone, because we like to meet everyone in person first. Thank you for listening, and enjoy your walk.

audio.t: Come in, Tomas and Hana. I have read your outline on classroom noise and reading. Tell me where you are with it.
We are quite happy with the idea. We want to see whether background noise in primary school classrooms affects how well children understand what they read.
Our first plan was to visit four schools, but we have started to worry that it is too much for one term.

You are right to worry. Two schools will be plenty, provided you choose them carefully. If both are in quiet suburbs, your results will tell us very little, so pick one on a main road and one in a calm area.
That makes sense. We could ask the council which schools are near the busiest roads.
Good. Now, how do you plan to measure the noise?
We were going to use a free app on our phones. It is cheap, and we can take it anywhere.

I would advise against it. Those apps are not accurate enough, and a reviewer will notice. The engineering department has calibrated sound meters, and they lend them to students for a few days. Ask for one early because they are popular.
Thank you. We also planned to write our own reading test, with short passages and questions.

That worries me more. Designing a fair test takes months. Use an existing standardized test, which has already been checked for reliability. It also means your results can be compared with other research.
That will save a lot of time. What about getting permission to work with children?

That is the biggest obstacle. You need approval from the ethics committee, and it meets only once a month. The next deadline for papers is the twelfth, so you have about two weeks. You will need consent letters for parents, and all the data must be anonymous.
We had not realized the deadline was so close. We will start on the letters tonight.
Another thing is the analysis. Neither of us is confident with statistics.
Few students are. There is a workshop on Thursday afternoons run by the library, and I strongly recommend it. Bring your own data if you can, because the tutor will help you choose the right test.
Should we do a small pilot study first?
Yes, a pilot in one classroom would show you problems before the real study, such as children finishing the test too quickly. It need not take long.
And the report itself? We have a limit of five thousand words.

Do not spend too long on the literature review. Two thousand words is enough, and many students go over. I would rather see a thoughtful section about the limitations of your study, because small samples have to be treated carefully.
That is useful. We will also send you a draft of the method section before the end of the month.
Please do. Send it by the twentieth, and I will reply within three days.

audio.t: Today I want to talk about bioluminescence, the production of light by living things. It is far more common than most people imagine. In the open ocean, roughly three-quarters of the animals living between the surface and the deep sea can make their own light, which suggests that it is one of the most widespread forms of communication on the planet.

The light comes from a chemical reaction. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and an enzyme named luciferase speeds the process up. The result is a cold light, which wastes almost no energy as heat. The color is usually blue or green, and there is a good reason for this. Blue-green light travels farther through seawater than any other color, so animals have evolved to use the wavelengths that work best.

Sunlight fades quickly in the sea. Below about two hundred meters there is very little of it left, and below one thousand meters the water is completely dark. In this environment, light becomes extremely valuable, and animals use it in at least three ways.

The first use is camouflage. Many fish and squid have light-producing organs on their undersides. Predators looking up see a faint glow that matches the dim light from above, so the animal's outline disappears. This is known as counter-illumination.

The second use is hunting. The best known example is the anglerfish, which dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth. Small fish are attracted to it and swim close enough to be caught. Some squid use a different trick. When threatened, they release a cloud of glowing liquid instead of ink, which confuses the attacker while they escape.

The third use is a kind of burglar alarm. Some tiny plankton flash when they are disturbed. This does not scare predators, but it attracts larger predators that may attack whatever is eating the plankton. So the small animal's flash is a call for help.

Not all bioluminescence is produced by the animal alone. The Hawaiian bobtail squid, for example, hosts glowing bacteria in a special organ. Each morning, the squid expels most of the bacteria and keeps only a small number, which then multiply during the day, ready for the night. The squid gains camouflage, and the bacteria receive food and shelter.

Researchers are interested in more than the biology. The proteins that create the glow have become useful laboratory tools. Scientists attach them to other molecules to see where and when particular genes are active, and some medical teams use the same method to track the spread of disease inside cells. It is a good example of a curiosity about nature leading to a practical benefit.

The second use is hunting. The best known example is the anglerfish, which dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth. Small fish are attracted to it and swim close enough to be caught. Some squid use a different trick. When threatened, they release a cloud of glowing liquid instead of ink, which confuses the attacker while they escape.

The third use is a kind of burglar alarm. Some tiny plankton flash when they are disturbed. This does not scare predators, but it attracts larger predators that may attack whatever is eating the plankton. So the small animal's flash is a call for help.

Not all bioluminescence is produced by the animal alone. The Hawaiian bobtail squid, for example, hosts glowing bacteria in a special organ. Each morning, the squid expels most of the bacteria and keeps only a small number, which then multiply during the day, ready for the night. The squid gains camouflage, and the bacteria receive food and shelter.

Researchers are interested in more than the biology. The proteins that create the glow have become useful laboratory tools. Scientists attach them to other molecules to see where and when particular genes are active, and some medical teams use the same method to track the spread of disease inside cells. It is a good example of a curiosity about nature leading to a practical benefit.

items.text:
Quantum Computing: Beyond the Bit
A. Every digital device in the world, from a pocket calculator to a weather-forecasting supercomputer, rests on the same humble idea: the bit. A bit is a switch that is either off or on, represented as 0 or 1, and every photograph, song and bank balance is ultimately a long string of these two symbols. For seventy years, progress in computing meant packing more switches onto a chip and making them flip faster. That strategy has been astonishingly successful, but its physical limits are now visible. Transistors in the most advanced chips are only a few dozen atoms wide, and at such scales the tidy rules of everyday electronics begin to break down. Quantum computing proposes to escape this impasse not by shrinking the switch further but by replacing it with something that obeys different rules entirely.
B. The replacement is the quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike an ordinary bit, a qubit can exist in a superposition, a blend of 0 and 1 that is resolved into one definite value only when it is measured. Popular accounts often claim that a qubit is "both 0 and 1 at once", but physicists regard this as a convenient simplification at best. A more accurate picture is that a qubit carries a pair of numbers, called amplitudes, that determine the probability of each outcome when the system is read. Crucially, these amplitudes can be positive or negative, which allows them to cancel one another, much as ripples on a pond can flatten each other when two waves meet. Quantum algorithms are essentially choreographies designed so that the amplitudes pointing to wrong answers cancel while those pointing to the right answer reinforce each other.
C. The second ingredient is entanglement, a correlation between qubits that has no counterpart in classical physics. When two qubits are entangled, the state of the pair cannot be described by describing each qubit separately; measuring one immediately tells you something about the other, however far apart they are. Entanglement does not allow messages to travel faster than light, a misconception that has persisted for decades, but it does allow a collection of qubits to represent an enormous range of possibilities in a compact way. To describe forty entangled qubits, a classical machine would need to store more than a trillion numbers, whereas the qubits themselves simply exist in that state.
D. None of this makes a quantum computer a faster version of a laptop, and here the hype has run ahead of the science. For most everyday tasks, such as word processing, streaming video or managing a spreadsheet, a quantum machine would offer no advantage whatsoever. Its promise lies in a narrow family of problems with a particular mathematical structure. The best known is the factoring of large numbers. In the 1990s a mathematician named Halvard Teague showed that a sufficiently large quantum computer could perform this task vastly faster than any known classical method. Because much of today's internet encryption relies on the difficulty of factoring, the result alarmed security experts and prompted the development of new codes designed to resist quantum attack. A second promising domain is simulation. Molecules are themselves quantum systems, and calculating how they behave is so demanding that chemists normally rely on approximations. A quantum computer could, in principle, model a catalyst or a drug molecule directly.
E. The obstacle is fragility. Qubits are so sensitive that stray heat, vibration or electromagnetic noise can destroy their delicate states in a fraction of a second, a problem known as decoherence. Engineers therefore cool many designs to temperatures colder than outer space and wrap them in layered shields. Even so, today's qubits make an error roughly once in every thousand operations, whereas an ordinary chip errs perhaps once in a billion billion. The answer is error correction: spreading a single logical piece of information across many physical qubits so that mistakes can be detected and repaired. The cost is steep. Current estimates suggest that one reliable logical qubit may require a thousand or more physical ones, which means that a machine capable of breaking modern encryption would need millions of qubits, compared with the few hundred in the largest devices today.
F. Several rival technologies are competing to supply those qubits. Superconducting circuits, favored by many large laboratories, are fast and can be manufactured with familiar techniques, but they demand extreme refrigeration. Trapped ions, individual charged atoms held in place by electric fields, are exceptionally stable and precise but operate more slowly. A third approach uses photons, particles of light, which suffer little from heat but are hard to make interact with one another. No consensus has emerged about which will prevail, and some researchers suspect that the eventual winner has not yet been invented. In a sign of how uncertain the field remains, several companies hedge their bets by funding more than one approach.
G. Sceptics reasonably ask whether the effort is justified. Dr Mireille Okonkwo-Hart, a physicist at the Varden Institute, argues that the strongest case is not any single application but the knowledge gained in learning to control nature at its smallest scale, in the same way that early research on electricity could not have predicted the telephone. Others are more cautious, pointing out that several once-promised technologies, nuclear fusion among them, have seemed to recede as they were approached. What is clear is that quantum computing will not arrive as a sudden revolution. It is more likely to emerge gradually, first as specialized accelerators used alongside conventional machines for chemistry and materials problems, and only much later, if ever, as a general-purpose tool.

items.text:
Two Tongues, One Brain
A. For much of the twentieth century, speaking two languages was regarded with suspicion by educators. Immigrant parents in many countries were advised to speak only the majority language at home, on the theory that a second tongue would confuse a child and delay learning. Early studies appeared to support this view, reporting that bilingual children scored lower on vocabulary tests than their monolingual peers. Only later did researchers notice that these studies had often compared children from poor immigrant families with children from affluent local ones, so that language was tangled up with income, schooling and many other factors. When such differences were controlled, the supposed deficit largely disappeared.
B. The modern reassessment began with an observation about attention. In a well-known series of experiments, the psychologist Dr Lena Havrik asked children to sort cards by color while ignoring a shape printed on each one, and then to switch the rule without warning. Bilingual children tended to adapt faster and to be less distracted by the misleading information. Havrik proposed an explanation that has shaped the field ever since. A bilingual speaker never fully switches one language off; both remain partly active, competing for selection, even when only one is being spoken. The brain must therefore keep choosing the right word and suppressing the rival, and this constant practice, she argued, strengthens a general-purpose system for control and attention that psychologists call executive function.
C. Brain imaging has added a physical dimension to the argument. In the Brevik Study, scans of two hundred adults found that those who had used two languages daily for many years had a denser layer of gray matter in regions associated with language selection and, in some cases, better-preserved white matter, the bundles of fibers that connect distant areas. The effect was strongest among people who had learned their second language early and used it constantly. These findings are suggestive rather than conclusive, however. Scans show that two groups differ; they cannot show why, and people who become bilingual may differ from others in ways that no one has measured.
D. The most striking claim concerns old age. Several studies of hospital records have reported that bilingual patients develop the symptoms of dementia four to five years later, on average, than monolingual patients. The favored explanation is cognitive reserve: a brain that has worked harder throughout life builds richer networks and can compensate for damage by routing activity through alternative pathways. Importantly, this does not mean that bilingualism prevents the disease, only that it may postpone the point at which damage becomes visible in behavior. Critics add a caution. In some regions, the people who migrate and learn another language may also be healthier, better educated and more resilient than those who stay, which would produce the same pattern without any help from language.
E. The strongest challenge has come from replication. Several large studies attempting to repeat Havrik's results found no advantage in bilingual children at all, and a meta-analysis led by the statistician Joaquim Corvin concluded that the published literature is skewed. Studies reporting a bilingual advantage, it found, were considerably more likely to reach print than studies reporting none, so the overall picture looked rosier than the evidence deserved. Defenders reply that bilingualism is not a single condition. A child who speaks one language at home and another at school, and who switches many times a day, may have a very different experience from one who uses a second language only in weekly lessons, and lumping them together may hide real effects.
F. Bilingualism also has costs, and these are less contested. Bilingual adults tend to be slightly slower at naming pictures and experience more tip-of-the-tongue moments, when a familiar word refuses to come. In either language taken on its own, their vocabulary is often a little smaller than a monolingual's, because their experience is divided between two. When the two vocabularies are added together, however, the total is usually equal or greater. Such differences are measured in fractions of a second and a handful of words, and few people notice them in daily life.
G. Where does this leave parents and teachers? The most sensible reading of the evidence is that the old fear has been laid to rest: raising a child with two languages does not harm development, and it brings obvious social and cultural rewards. Whether it also delivers a broad cognitive boost is still unresolved. Some researchers now suggest that the more productive question is not whether bilingualism makes people smarter but how the brain manages two languages and how that management varies with age, use and context. If that shift of emphasis succeeds, the field may finally replace slogans with understanding.

items.text:
The Long Flight of the Monarch
A. Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave the cool north of the continent and travel as far as four thousand kilometers to a handful of mountain forests in central Mexico. The journey would be remarkable for any animal, but the monarch weighs less than a paperclip and has a brain the size of a grain of sand. More surprising still, no individual makes the round trip. The butterflies that arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those that left it the previous spring, and they find the same trees that their ancestors rested in, without a map or a guide.
B. The explanation begins with an unusual life cycle. Over the course of a year, the eastern population produces four or five generations. Those that hatch in spring and early summer live only two to six weeks, mating, laying eggs on milkweed and moving gradually north. The generation that emerges in late summer is different. Triggered by shortening days and cooler nights, these butterflies enter a state called reproductive diapause, in which their reproductive organs remain dormant. Freed from the demands of egg-laying, they live eight months or more, long enough to fly south, survive the winter and set off north again in spring. Biologists sometimes call this generation the "Methuselah" butterflies, after the legendary figure said to have lived for centuries.
C. How these inexperienced insects find their way is one of the great puzzles of animal behavior. Part of the answer is a sun compass. Monarchs track the position of the sun and correct for its movement across the sky using an internal clock, whose genes are active in their antennae. In laboratory experiments led by Dr Tobias Ankerman, butterflies whose antennae had been painted black could not tell time properly and flew in random directions, whereas those with clear paint kept their course. The sun cannot be the whole story, since monarchs continue in the right direction under heavy cloud. Research suggests that they can also sense the angle of the Earth's magnetic field, an ability that may serve as a backup when the sun is hidden.
D. At the end of the journey, the butterflies gather in forests of oyamel fir trees at altitudes of about three thousand meters. They cluster by the thousands on single branches, so densely that the boughs bend under their weight. The forest is crucial. Its canopy acts like an umbrella, keeping rain from soaking the insects, and like a blanket, holding in warmth on clear nights. The temperature inside the clusters stays just above freezing, cold enough to slow the butterflies' metabolism so that their stored fat lasts all winter, but warm enough to avoid ice forming in their bodies. A site that is too warm would force them to burn their reserves too quickly; one that is too exposed could kill them in a single storm.
E. In March the survivors become active, mate, and fly north to Texas and neighboring states, where they lay eggs on newly growing milkweed. Then they die, and their offspring continue the journey. Milkweed is essential at this stage because it is the only plant on which monarch caterpillars can feed. The plant contains toxins that the caterpillars store in their bodies, making the adult butterflies unpleasant to birds, a warning advertised by their bright orange wings.
F. Not all monarchs go to Mexico. A separate western population, which lives beyond the Rocky Mountains, spends the winter in groves of pine and eucalyptus trees along the California coast. Its numbers have fallen sharply in recent decades, and the reasons are still debated. Farther south, in warm regions such as Florida and the Caribbean, some monarchs stay all year and never migrate at all. These populations are a reminder that the species as a whole is not in immediate danger of extinction.
G. The eastern population is nonetheless in trouble. Scientists measure its size by the area of forest the butterflies occupy each winter, which reached about eighteen hectares in the mid-1990s and had fallen to less than one hectare by 2013. Several pressures act together: the loss of milkweed as farmers adopt herbicides that kill weeds in and around fields, illegal logging in the Mexican forests, and extreme weather that can disrupt both the journey and the winter shelter. Nobody has been able to say which of these matters most, and they probably vary from year to year.
H. Conservation efforts have therefore been broad. Gardeners and schools plant milkweed in backyards and along roads, and volunteers in the Longmere Tagging Network attach tiny stickers to wings and report where the butterflies are found, filling gaps that no professional team could cover. Yet the writer Ines Marchetti has argued that the real object of concern is not the monarch itself but its migration. A species can survive as a resident population, she points out; the long journey, however, is an inherited behavior that, once broken, cannot easily be restored. In that sense, what is at risk is less a butterfly than one of the most extraordinary phenomena in the natural world.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 1. Nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visitors, in thousands, to the main museum in each of four cities in 2010 and 2024, together with the percentage of 2024 visitors who were under 25 years old.
Aldermere: 420 thousand visitors in 2010; 515 thousand in 2024; 38% under 25.
Brenton: 610 thousand in 2010; 480 thousand in 2024; 21% under 25.
Corvale: 150 thousand in 2010; 390 thousand in 2024; 57% under 25.
Dunmarsh: 305 thousand in 2010; 310 thousand in 2024; 29% under 25.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares visitor numbers at the main museum in four cities in 2010 and 2024 and shows what share of visitors in the later year were under 25. Overall, three of the museums grew or stayed level, while only one lost visitors, and the strongest growth was linked to the youngest audiences.
Corvale recorded by far the most dramatic change. Its visitors rose from 150 thousand to 390 thousand, more than doubling, and 57% of them were under 25, the highest proportion in the table. Aldermere also grew, from 420 thousand to 515 thousand, and just over a third of its visitors (38%) were young people.
In contrast, Brenton was the only museum to lose visitors. It had the largest audience in 2010, at 610 thousand, but this fell by 130 thousand to 480 thousand, and it also had the lowest share of under-25s, at only 21%. Dunmarsh was almost unchanged, edging up from 305 thousand to 310 thousand, with 29% of its visitors under 25.
In summary, the museums that attracted most young people were those that expanded most, whereas the city with the oldest audience saw a decline.
items.vi: Mô tả bảng số liệu: nêu xu hướng chính (Corvale tăng mạnh nhất, Brenton giảm), so sánh các thành phố và có câu tổng quan.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 2. Nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này.

items.q: Some people believe that governments should spend public money on space exploration. Others think that this money would be better used to solve problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
Space programs cost enormous sums, and it is natural that many taxpayers ask whether the money could be better used closer to home. While some people argue that exploration is a luxury, others believe it brings lasting benefits. In my opinion, both views contain truth, but a modest level of investment in space is justified.
Those who oppose spending on space point to urgent needs on Earth. Millions of people still lack clean water, adequate housing or basic medical care, and a single launch can cost as much as a new hospital. It seems hard to defend sending a probe to a distant planet when children in some regions go hungry. Moreover, governments have limited budgets, and every dollar spent on rockets is a dollar not spent on schools or roads.
However, supporters of exploration make a strong case. Many technologies that we now take for granted, from satellite weather forecasts to navigation systems and lightweight medical materials, were developed through space research. Satellites also monitor deforestation, pollution and rising sea levels, so they directly help us to solve problems on Earth. In addition, space missions inspire young people to study science and engineering, which strengthens a country's economy over the long term. Finally, there is the argument of curiosity: understanding the origin of the solar system is part of understanding our own planet.
On balance, I believe the choice is not as stark as it appears. Space budgets are usually a tiny fraction of national spending, so reducing them would free up very little money for other purposes. A sensible government would therefore protect the most practical projects, such as Earth observation, while avoiding expensive missions whose main goal is prestige. International cooperation can also reduce the cost of each country.
In conclusion, space exploration and social spending are not true opposites. If budgets are kept reasonable and focused on projects with clear public benefits, a country can look to the stars without turning its back on its own people.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the examiner's questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Do you enjoy reading? What kind of things do you like to read?
items.sample: Yes, I really enjoy reading, especially science magazines and short stories, because they help me relax after a long day and I often learn something new.
items.vi: Nói em có thích đọc không và thích đọc gì, kèm lý do.

items.q: How do you usually spend your mornings?
items.sample: In the morning I usually get up at six thirty and have a quick breakfast. Then I check my messages and walk to the bus stop, which takes about ten minutes.
items.vi: Kể buổi sáng thường ngày của em.

items.q: Do you like taking photographs? Why or why not?
items.sample: I do like taking photographs because they keep my memories alive. I mostly photograph my friends and interesting buildings, and I sometimes share the best ones online.
items.vi: Trả lời em có thích chụp ảnh không và giải thích.

items.q: What is the weather like in your hometown in winter?
items.sample: The weather in my hometown in winter is usually cold and rather damp. It rarely snows, but there is a lot of fog in the mornings, so I always wear a warm coat.
items.vi: Mô tả thời tiết quê em vào mùa đông.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1-2 phút.

items.q: Describe a museum or gallery that you have visited. You should say: where it was and when you went; what you saw there; who you went with; and explain whether you would recommend it to other people.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a science museum that I visited in the capital last spring. I went there with my cousin and two of her friends, because she was studying for an exam in physics and wanted to see some real experiments. The museum is housed in an old factory, which I thought was interesting in itself, with huge windows and a high metal roof. The first thing that I noticed was a giant pendulum that swung slowly over the entrance hall and showed how the Earth turns. After that we spent most of our time in the space gallery, where there was a real capsule that astronauts had used. We could even sit inside it, and I was surprised at how tiny it was. My favorite section was the hands-on lab, where visitors could build small electric circuits and test them. I would certainly recommend this museum to other people because it explains difficult ideas in a clear and enjoyable way, and the staff were friendly and happy to answer our questions. The ticket was a little expensive, but I felt that it was good value, and I would happily go back again.
items.vi: Mô tả một bảo tàng đã đến: ở đâu, thấy gì, đi với ai và có giới thiệu không; nói liền mạch 1-2 phút.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss these more abstract questions with the examiner.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng hơn với giám khảo.

items.q: Why do you think some people prefer visiting museums to reading about history in books?
items.sample: I think some people prefer museums because they can see real objects, and that makes history feel more alive. Reading about a sword or a painting is not the same as standing next to it. Also, museums often include sound and film, which make the past easier to imagine.
items.vi: Giải thích vì sao nhiều người thích đến bảo tàng hơn là đọc sách lịch sử.

items.q: Should museums be free for everyone? What are the advantages and disadvantages?
items.sample: In my opinion museums should be free, because an important advantage is that everyone, including poorer families, can learn from them. However, running a museum is expensive, so the government would need to pay more, or the museum might have to reduce its collections and staff.
items.vi: Nêu ưu nhược điểm của việc bảo tàng miễn phí.

items.q: How might technology change the way people experience museums in the future?
items.sample: I think technology will change museums a lot in the future. Visitors will probably use virtual reality to walk through ancient cities, and apps will explain each object in their own language. On the other hand, I hope people will still want to see real objects in person.
items.vi: Dự đoán công nghệ sẽ thay đổi trải nghiệm bảo tàng như thế nào.

audio.t: Good morning, Heathbridge Steam Railway, group bookings. How can I help?
Morning. I would like to arrange a trip for our local history society.
Certainly. Can I take a surname for the booking?
Yes, it is Teasdale, that is T-E-A-S-D-A-L-E.
Thank you, Mr Teasdale. Which date were you thinking of?
We hoped for Saturday the fourteenth of June, but I suppose that is a busy weekend.
It is, I am afraid. We are full that day. The following Saturday, the twenty-first, still has space.
Then the twenty-first, please.
And how many people will be coming?
Twenty, but two of them may drop out, so let us say eighteen for now.

That is fine. Groups of fifteen or more get a reduced rate. There are two kinds of ticket. Standard is in open carriages. Heritage class has restored nineteen-thirties compartments with tables and windows that open.
Heritage sounds right. Most of our members are retired and they like a bit of comfort.
Heritage is normally twenty-four dollars per person, but with the group reduction it will be twenty.
That is very reasonable.
The train does not leave from the main station at the moment because of engineering works. It leaves from Alderley Halt, about ten minutes away by taxi.
Alderley, I see. And is lunch included?
You can have either a hot lunch or a cold buffet. The hot lunch needs two weeks' notice, so I am afraid it is only the cold buffet for the twenty-first.
Cold is fine. Oh, one more thing. One of our members uses a wheelchair. Is that a problem?
Not at all. The heritage carriages have no ramp, but we have a special wagon with a lift, which we will reserve for you.
Wonderful. Should I give you my phone number? It is oh-seven-seven-one-four, then four-oh-six-seven.
Four-oh-six-seven, thank you. Finally, we ask for a deposit of twenty-five percent. Could you send it by the end of next week?
I will post a cheque on Monday.
That might be too late, because it must reach us by Friday, so a bank transfer would be safer.
Then I will do a transfer. Thank you very much.

audio.t: Good evening, and welcome to this briefing for new stallholders at the Linden Quay Night Market. My name is Priya Raman and I manage the market for the Quay Trust.

Let me start with the venue. Many of you expected the market to be on the riverside promenade, and that was indeed the first plan. However, a survey showed that the promenade floods several times a year after heavy rain, so we have moved to the upper floor of the old grain warehouse. It is a little smaller, but it has a good roof and strong lighting, and it can be reached by a lift as well as by stairs.

The market will open on Friday and Saturday evenings, from five until ten. We had planned to open on Thursdays as well, but traders told us that midweek trade would be weak, so we dropped it. We may reconsider in the summer.

Now the stalls. There are sixty pitches in total. Thirty are for food, because our research suggests that most visitors come to eat. Twelve are for crafts, and the rest are for what we call pop-up traders, people who want to test a new product for a few weeks before committing to a regular pitch. If you are in that last group you are welcome to apply, but you must book a week ahead.

Now, money. Traders pay by the night, not by the month. A food pitch costs forty-five dollars a night and a craft pitch costs thirty. In addition, we ask for a deposit of fifty dollars. You will get it back at the end of the season, provided that your pitch has been left clean after every night.

Next, equipment. Each pitch has one electric socket, and the building's supply is limited. Gas cooking is not allowed at all, so food traders will need electric hotplates. I know this is a big change if you are used to street markets, but the fire regulations for an indoor venue are very strict.

On waste, we are a plastic-free market. We have set up a bulk-buying scheme for compostable plates and cutlery, and it will cost you less than buying them yourselves. You are asked to use only items from that scheme.

Setting up. You may enter the building from three o'clock. The lift is reserved for deliveries until half past four, after which it is open to the public, so please bring heavy items early. Cars cannot be parked inside, but there is a loading bay at the rear where you can stop for fifteen minutes.

Publicity. We will advertise on local radio and put up posters on buses, but in last year's pilot the most effective method was free samples. Each trader gave out small tastes or demonstrations, and visitors told their friends. So please budget for some samples.

The pilot gave us useful feedback. Seventy percent of visitors said they would come again. The main complaint was not the prices or the crowds, but the lack of seating, so we have added a seating area near the lift.

Finally, if you have a problem during opening hours, please do not telephone the office, which closes at five. Speak to the duty supervisor, who wears a green jacket and will be near the main entrance. Thank you, and I look forward to seeing you all on opening night.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, your project is about background music and studying. Tell me where you have got to.
Well, Dr Whitlock, we are a bit worried that the topic has been done to death. There is so much already written about it.

There is, but that is actually in your favor. The results of earlier studies point in completely different directions. Some found that music helps, some that it harms, and a few found no effect at all, so there is still plenty to clarify.
That is what we noticed. We also wanted to use a proper lab, but the psychology lab is only free during the day, when most of our volunteers are in classes.
Then use a seminar room in the evening. Just keep conditions identical for every participant, with the same lighting and the same seating.
We were thinking of four conditions: silence, instrumental music, music with lyrics, and nature sounds.
I would drop the nature sounds. With only thirty participants you will struggle to make sense of four conditions, so three is plenty.
All right. For the reading task we have written some passages and a twenty-question test afterwards. We tried it on a few friends and all of them scored above ninety percent.
Then the test is too easy. You will not see any difference between conditions if everyone is at the top of the scale. Add some questions that require inference rather than simple recall.
Right. And each participant will do all three conditions, with different passages each time.
Good, but vary the order. Otherwise any difference might simply reflect tiredness or practice rather than the music.
Should people bring their own headphones?
No, you should supply them and set the volume yourselves. If participants choose their own volume, the results will not be comparable.
One more problem. Several volunteers told us they always study with music on, and that could bias things.
Ask about it in a short questionnaire, and treat it as a separate factor in your analysis. Do not exclude those people, because you would lose too much data.
We will also need a consent form. Is there anything special we should include?
Make it clear that participants may stop at any time and may withdraw their data afterwards. Many students remember the first point and forget the second.
We planned to collect all the data in two weeks in March.
I think that is optimistic. Volunteers cancel, and you will lose days to timetable clashes. Allow three weeks.
And what should we hand in?
A one-page proposal by Friday, saying what you aim to find out, how you will test it and how you will analyze the results. Do not worry about the literature review yet. That comes later.

Earlier studies have produced conflicting results.
Very little research has been done on it.

audio.t: Today I want to look at seaweed farming, a form of aquaculture that has expanded rapidly over the past twenty years.
The world now produces more than thirty million tonnes of seaweed every year, and about ninety percent of it is grown in Asia, although interest is growing in Europe and North America.

What makes seaweed unusual is how little it needs. Unlike fish farming, it requires no feed, because it takes nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus directly from the sea water. It needs no fresh water and no fertilizer either.

A typical farm works like this. The young plants begin life in a hatchery, where tiny spores are attached to string. The string is then taken out to sea and fixed to long lines anchored in shallow water. The lines are held at a depth of about two meters, so that the plants receive plenty of light.
Growth is rapid. For many species, the crop is ready to harvest after only three months, and in warm conditions farmers can take several crops a year.

Food is still the biggest market, but other uses are growing. In trials, adding small amounts of one red seaweed to the diet of cattle has reduced the methane that the animals produce by up to eighty percent. Another promising use is packaging. Films made from seaweed are fully biodegradable, so they break down within weeks instead of lasting for centuries like plastic.

Of course there are challenges. The first is the weather. Farms need sheltered bays, because storms can tear lines from their anchors and destroy a season's work. A second problem is warming sea water, since heat waves can kill a crop within days. And finally, in Europe and America there is a shortage of processing plants, which means that farmers often have nowhere to sell what they grow.
