audio.t: Today I want to look at seaweed farming, a form of aquaculture that has expanded rapidly over the past twenty years.
The world now produces more than thirty million tonnes of seaweed every year, and about ninety percent of it is grown in Asia, although interest is growing in Europe and North America.

What makes seaweed unusual is how little it needs. Unlike fish farming, it requires no feed, because it takes nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus directly from the sea water. It needs no fresh water and no fertilizer either.

A typical farm works like this. The young plants begin life in a hatchery, where tiny spores are attached to string. The string is then taken out to sea and fixed to long lines anchored in shallow water. The lines are held at a depth of about two meters, so that the plants receive plenty of light.
Growth is rapid. For many species, the crop is ready to harvest after only three months, and in warm conditions farmers can take several crops a year.

Food is still the biggest market, but other uses are growing. In trials, adding small amounts of one red seaweed to the diet of cattle has reduced the methane that the animals produce by up to eighty percent. Another promising use is packaging. Films made from seaweed are fully biodegradable, so they break down within weeks instead of lasting for centuries like plastic.

Of course there are challenges. The first is the weather. Farms need sheltered bays, because storms can tear lines from their anchors and destroy a season's work. A second problem is warming sea water, since heat waves can kill a crop within days. And finally, in Europe and America there is a shortage of processing plants, which means that farmers often have nowhere to sell what they grow.

items.text:
Who Answers for the Algorithm?
A. For most of the twentieth century, a decision about a loan, a job or a prison sentence was made by a person who could be asked to explain it. Today, a growing share of such decisions begins with a statistical model that sorts applicants into categories, ranks them and, in many cases, recommends an outcome. Supporters argue that this shift removes the whims, moods and prejudices of individual officials. Critics reply that it has merely relocated those prejudices, burying them in code and in the historical records on which the code was trained, where they are far harder to see and to contest.
B. The central difficulty is that an algorithm learns from the past. A hiring tool developed by the Marlowe Group was trained on ten years of recruitment records, and it duly learned that the firm had mostly promoted men. Although the designers deleted gender from the data, the model found proxies: membership of certain sports clubs, the names of some colleges, even gaps in employment history. Its recommendations reproduced the old pattern with impressive consistency. Nobody had instructed it to discriminate. It had simply been rewarded for resembling the firm's earlier choices, and those choices were the problem.
C. Technical remedies exist, but they force uncomfortable choices. Computer scientists have proposed several mathematical definitions of fairness: that error rates should be equal across groups, that a given score should mean the same level of risk for everyone, or that favorable outcomes should be distributed in proportion to each group's share of the population. Researchers have shown that, except in unusual circumstances, these definitions cannot all be satisfied at once. Choosing among them is therefore not a technical matter but a moral one, and it matters who makes the choice. In practice it is often made quietly, by engineers working to a deadline, without any public discussion.
D. Transparency is frequently offered as the answer, yet it is less straightforward than it sounds. Some of the most accurate models, particularly deep neural networks, are opaque even to their creators: they can report what they predict but not why, in terms that a human could verify. Companies also resist disclosure on commercial grounds, arguing that revealing the workings of a model would let competitors copy it and let applicants game it. Legal scholars have responded by distinguishing between explaining a model as a whole and explaining a single decision. A rejected applicant, they argue, does not need the mathematics. She needs to know which factors counted against her and what she might change.
E. A second line of defense is human oversight, but the evidence suggests it is weaker than hoped. In a study of caseworkers in the Danvers region, who received risk scores for the families on their lists, the officials overruled the software in fewer than one case in twenty, even when the score contradicted their own notes. Psychologists call this automation bias: the tendency to treat a machine's output as more objective than one's own judgment. Where a human merely signs off on a recommendation, responsibility becomes diffuse. The official can say that the system advised it, the developer can say that the official decided, and the person affected finds nobody to whom an appeal can be addressed.
F. Some governments have begun to experiment with audits. Regulators in several jurisdictions now require impact assessments before high-stakes systems are deployed, much as environmental assessments precede a new road. Independent auditors test the system on sample data and publish their findings. Sceptics note that auditors depend on access that companies may restrict, and that a system which passes an audit today may drift as its data changes. Others worry that a requirement for extensive paperwork will favor large firms that can afford compliance departments, leaving small developers, and the public services that rely on them, with a heavier burden.
G. Perhaps the most striking proposal comes from a different direction: to ask what an algorithm is for. A model that predicts which tenants are likely to fall behind with their rent can be used to deny them housing or to offer early help with payments. The mathematics is identical, but the ethics are not. Several philosophers therefore argue that scrutiny should focus less on the accuracy of predictions than on the purposes and consequences attached to them. By this reasoning, the most important question is not whether a system is biased in some abstract sense, but who gains from it, who bears the risk of its errors, and who has the power to say no.

items.text:
The Ground Gives Way
A. Permafrost, ground that remains at or below freezing for at least two consecutive years, underlies roughly a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere. Much of it has been frozen since the last ice age, and in places it extends hundreds of meters down. For the communities built upon it, from fishing villages to mining towns, it has long been the most reliable of foundations. Over recent decades, however, measurements taken in deep boreholes have shown steady warming, and in some Arctic locations ground temperatures have risen by two or three degrees Celsius. The ground is not yet melting everywhere, but it is no longer as cold as it was.
B. The most visible consequence is structural. Ice wedges and ice-rich soil lose volume when they thaw, and the surface subsides unevenly. Roads buckle, pipelines sag and buildings tilt as their pilings lose their grip. In the town of Tarsuk, a school built in 1974 on piles driven into frozen silt has needed its foundations jacked up three times since 2005. A regional study projects that, by the middle of the century, the cost of maintaining northern roads and buildings could rise by around a fifth. Such figures are estimates, but engineers who work in the region regard them as conservative, because damage tends to accelerate once a slope or a road bed begins to fail.
C. Less visible, but potentially more consequential, is what the thawing soil releases. Frozen ground holds vast quantities of organic matter, the remains of plants and animals that accumulated over thousands of years and decayed only slowly in the cold. Northern permafrost is thought to contain roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere does today. When it thaws, microbes begin to digest this material, producing carbon dioxide where oxygen is plentiful and methane where the ground is waterlogged. Methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over a period of a few decades, although it breaks down in the air faster, so its effect is intense but shorter lived.
D. Scientists disagree about how quickly the carbon will escape. Gradual thaw, in which the upper layer of soil deepens by a few centimeters each year, is relatively well understood and can be represented in climate models. Abrupt thaw is a different matter. In regions rich in ground ice, the soil can collapse within weeks, forming hollows and lakes known as thermokarst, and exposing deep deposits to decay far faster than most models have assumed. A team led by the ecologist Mei Halvorsen estimated that abrupt thaw, although it affects only about a fifth of permafrost land, could release carbon in quantities that roughly double the warming effect of the gradual process alone. Not every specialist accepts so large a figure, but few now dispute that the abrupt process has been underestimated.
E. Thaw also changes what grows. Warmer soils allow shrubs to spread across the tundra, and some researchers have argued that this new vegetation, which absorbs carbon through photosynthesis, could offset a large part of what the soil loses. There is a complication, however. Dark shrubs absorb more sunlight than snow-covered ground, so their spread warms the surface further. Field measurements so far offer little support for a full offset. At most of the sites studied, the carbon released from the soil during the long winter exceeded what the new plants absorbed during the short summer. The balance may change as growth continues, but at present the landscape is losing carbon rather than gaining it.
F. The effects reach beyond the climate. Thawing ground can release old pollutants, including mercury that has been stored in frozen soils for millennia, and it may wash them into rivers on which communities depend for fish and drinking water. Where coastlines are made of ice-rich permafrost, waves undercut the softened bluffs and erosion can exceed ten meters a year, which is why Tarsuk is now planning to relocate part of its settlement inland. Relocation is expensive, but its costs are not purely financial. Residents have spoken of the loss of graves, fishing grounds and the places that anchor their sense of who they are.
G. Responses fall into two broad groups. Adaptation includes cooling devices called thermosyphons, which draw heat out of the ground beneath buildings, and houses raised on frames so that cold air can circulate beneath them. These measures protect individual structures but cannot save a whole landscape. Mitigation, meaning the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, can slow the thaw, yet because deep ground responds slowly to changes in air temperature, a share of the thaw is already unavoidable. Policy adds a further difficulty. Emissions from thawing permafrost are rarely included in national targets, so a country may meet its commitments on paper while its northern soils quietly work against them.

items.text:
Letters to the World: The Making of the Scientific Journal
A. Before the middle of the seventeenth century, natural philosophers shared discoveries mainly through private letters and expensive books. A letter reached only its recipient, who might or might not pass it on, and a book could take years to write and print. Scholars who wanted credit for an idea faced an awkward choice: to publish quickly and risk errors, or to wait and risk being forestalled. Some resorted to anagrams, publishing a scrambled sentence that could be unscrambled later to prove that they had got there first. The system worked for small circles of correspondents, but it was slow, and it depended entirely on goodwill.
B. In 1665 two periodicals appeared within weeks of each other. The Journal des Savants, begun in Paris in January, was largely a review of new books and a record of scholarly news. The Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, launched in London in March by the society's secretary, Henry Oldenburg, was different in spirit. It printed original observations, experiments and reports from correspondents abroad. Oldenburg ran it as a private venture, hoping to earn an income from sales, and the Royal Society itself did not accept financial responsibility for the journal until 1752.
C. What made the new format valuable was less speed than certainty. An article appeared with a date and a printed name, creating a public record of who had reported what, and when. Oldenburg understood the importance of this, and he sometimes assured authors that registering a result in the Transactions would protect their claim against rivals. The journal therefore did something that no private letter could do. It turned a discovery into a public, dated and attributable contribution, and it taught researchers to regard publication as the point at which an idea became their own and, at the same time, everyone's to test.
D. The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries saw journals multiply. As disciplines such as chemistry, geology and physiology separated from natural philosophy, each acquired its own societies and its own periodicals. Language shifted too. Latin gradually gave way to French, German and English, which widened the readership beyond the classically educated but also fragmented it. General journals survived alongside the specialist ones. Nature, founded in London in 1869, set out to bring news of science to educated readers of every background, a role that it later narrowed to that of a leading research journal.
E. Quality control was slower to develop than most modern readers assume. Editors had always sought advice from knowledgeable friends, and in 1752 the Royal Society formalized the practice by asking a committee to review papers before they were printed. Yet this was exceptional, and for most of the next two centuries decisions rested with editors alone. Even in the twentieth century, resistance could be fierce. In 1936, Albert Einstein, whose manuscript had been sent to a specialist for comment without his knowledge, withdrew it from the journal Physical Review in annoyance and published it elsewhere. Systematic peer review became standard only after the Second World War, when governments began to fund research on a vast scale and editors were overwhelmed by submissions that they could no longer judge alone.
F. The postwar boom also changed who owned journals. Commercial publishers, recognizing that libraries would subscribe to any title their researchers needed, built highly profitable businesses on content supplied free by authors and checked free by reviewers. From the 1970s, subscription prices rose faster than library budgets, a situation that librarians came to call the serials crisis. Universities found themselves paying twice for the products of their own staff: first through salaries, and then through subscriptions.
G. Measurement added another layer. In the 1960s, the American information scientist Eugene Garfield devised the impact factor, an average of the number of times a journal's recent articles are cited elsewhere. It was intended as a tool to help librarians decide which titles to buy. Over time, however, it came to be used to judge individual scientists, so that the prestige of a paper might depend more on where it appeared than on what it said. Many researchers now regard this as a distortion, and several funding bodies have pledged to stop using the measure in decisions about hiring and promotion.
H. Digital technology has loosened the journal's grip without ending it. Since 1991, physicists and later other scientists have posted drafts on preprint servers before any review, making distribution almost instantaneous and free. Open-access models, in which authors or funders pay for publication so that readers do not have to, have grown rapidly, although they have brought problems of their own, including low-quality outlets that will publish almost anything for a fee. Some commentators conclude that the journal's two original jobs, distribution and certification, have now come apart. Distribution is cheap and nearly universal. Certification, the assurance that a result has been scrutinized by qualified peers, remains scarce, and that, perhaps, is what the journal has left to sell.

Authors began to demand payment for their articles.
Libraries stopped subscribing to commercial journals.
Journal subscription prices increased more quickly than library budgets.

Open-access publishing has solved the problems of cost.

items.vi: Đoạn G: hệ số ảnh hưởng ban đầu cho thủ thư, sau dùng đánh giá nhà khoa học.

items.q: Which paragraph explains why separate scientific fields created their own journals?
items.vi: Đoạn D: các ngành tách khỏi triết học tự nhiên và lập hội và tạp chí riêng.

items.vi: Đoạn A: dùng đảo chữ (anagram) để chứng minh mình đến trước.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 1. Nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visits to the public library, in thousands, and the number of e-book loans, in thousands, in four towns in 2010 and in 2024.
Ashby: library visits 210 in 2010 and 148 in 2024; e-book loans 5 in 2010 and 96 in 2024.
Cresswick: library visits 95 in 2010 and 102 in 2024; e-book loans 2 in 2010 and 41 in 2024.
Dunmore: library visits 330 in 2010 and 205 in 2024; e-book loans 8 in 2010 and 170 in 2024.
Elmford: library visits 120 in 2010 and 61 in 2024; e-book loans 3 in 2010 and 19 in 2024.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares library visits and e-book loans in four towns in 2010 and 2024. Overall, physical visits fell in three of the towns, while e-book loans rose sharply everywhere.
Dunmore had the highest figures in both years. Its visits dropped from 330,000 to 205,000, yet its e-book loans grew from only 8,000 to 170,000, the largest increase in the table. Ashby followed a similar pattern, with visits down from 210,000 to 148,000 and loans rising from 5,000 to 96,000, so that e-books in 2024 were nearly two thirds as common as visits.
The two smaller towns were different. Cresswick was the only town where visits actually rose, edging up from 95,000 to 102,000, and its loans increased from 2,000 to 41,000. Elmford, in contrast, saw visits halve from 120,000 to 61,000, and its e-book loans reached just 19,000, the lowest figure in 2024. In summary, digital borrowing has grown strongly, but it has replaced physical visits in some towns and not in others.
items.vi: Mô tả bảng số liệu: nêu xu hướng chính (lượt đến thư viện giảm, mượn sách điện tử tăng mạnh), so sánh các thị trấn và có câu tổng quan.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 2. Nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này.

items.q: Some people think that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking, managing money and basic repairs. Others believe that schools should concentrate on academic subjects and leave practical skills to parents. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether schools should teach practical skills or concentrate on academic subjects. In my opinion, schools should do both, although academic learning should remain the priority.
Those who favor academic subjects make a reasonable point. Teachers are trained to teach mathematics, science and languages, and the time in a school day is limited. If lessons on cooking or repairs replaced history or physics, students might leave school without the knowledge needed for university or for skilled work. Supporters of this view also argue that parents are better placed to teach practical skills, because they can demonstrate them at home, in a real kitchen or workshop, and at a pace that suits each child.
However, this argument ignores the fact that not every family can provide such teaching. Some parents work long hours, and others never learned these skills themselves. As a result, young adults often leave home unable to cook a healthy meal or to understand a loan agreement, and the consequences can include poor diet and serious debt. A short, compulsory course on managing money, for example, would give every student the same basic protection, whatever their background.
Practical lessons can also support academic ones. Cooking involves measurement and chemistry, while budgeting is applied mathematics, and students who see a purpose in their learning often become more motivated. Moreover, many pupils who struggle in traditional lessons discover confidence when they succeed at making or repairing something.
For these reasons, I believe that schools should include a modest amount of practical teaching, perhaps one lesson a week, while keeping academic subjects at the center of the curriculum. Parents can then build on this foundation at home. In this way, young people would gain both knowledge and the ability to look after themselves.
items.vi: Bài thảo luận hai quan điểm: nêu cả hai phía (dạy kỹ năng thực hành ở trường và tập trung môn học thuật), đưa ý kiến riêng rõ ràng, có ví dụ và kết luận.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the examiner's questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Tell me about the room where you usually do your homework.
items.sample: I usually do my homework in my bedroom because it is quiet. I have a small desk by the window, so I get plenty of daylight, and I keep my books on a shelf above it.
items.vi: Mô tả phòng em học bài và lý do chọn nơi đó.

items.q: Do you prefer to plan your day or to do things spontaneously?
items.sample: I prefer to plan my day because it helps me stay calm. I write a short list every morning, although I also like leaving some free time for things that happen unexpectedly.
items.vi: Nói em thích lên kế hoạch hay tùy hứng, kèm lý do.

items.q: How do you keep in touch with friends who live far away?
items.sample: I usually send messages to my friends who live far away, and we sometimes have a video call at the weekend. It is not the same as meeting in person, but it keeps us close.
items.vi: Nói cách em giữ liên lạc với bạn ở xa.

items.q: What was the last photograph you took, and why did you take it?
items.sample: The last photograph I took was of a sunset from my classroom window. I took it because the sky was a beautiful orange color, and I wanted to show it to my sister.
items.vi: Kể về bức ảnh gần nhất em chụp và lý do.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1-2 phút.

items.q: Describe an important decision you made. You should say: what the decision was; why you had to make it; who you talked to about it; and explain how you feel about the decision now.
items.sample: I would like to talk about the decision I made last year to change schools. Until then I had studied at a small school near my house, but I wanted to join a school with a stronger science program. I had to decide because the application deadline was in March, and I could not wait any longer. At first I felt very nervous, because I would have to leave my friends and travel for an hour every day. I talked to my parents, and I also asked my cousin for advice, because she had made a similar move two years before. She told me that the first month would be difficult but that it would be worth it. In the end, I accepted the place. Now I am happy with my choice. I have made new friends, I enjoy my laboratory lessons, and I have learned to organize my time better. If I had stayed, I think I would have always wondered what might have happened.
items.vi: Kể về một quyết định quan trọng: đó là gì, vì sao phải quyết định, đã hỏi ai, và hiện giờ cảm thấy thế nào.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss these more abstract questions with the examiner.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng hơn với giám khảo.

items.q: Do you think people make big decisions with their heads or with their hearts?
items.sample: I think people usually use a mixture of both. Logic helps them compare the facts, such as the cost or the risks, but emotions often decide the final choice, especially in personal matters like where to live or whom to marry. People who use only logic can feel unhappy later, while people who follow only their feelings may regret it.
items.vi: Thảo luận người ta quyết định bằng lý trí hay cảm xúc; nêu cả hai phía.

items.q: Should young people be allowed to make their own decisions about their education?
items.sample: I believe young people should have a say, but parents should still guide them. Teenagers who choose their own subjects often feel more responsibility and work harder. However, they may not understand future job markets, so advice from parents and teachers is important. Making some mistakes is also part of learning.
items.vi: Nêu ý kiến về việc thanh thiếu niên tự quyết định chuyện học.

items.q: Does modern technology make decision-making easier or more difficult?
items.sample: In some ways it is easier, because we can find information and read reviews in seconds before buying something or choosing a course. On the other hand, there is sometimes too much information, which can feel overwhelming, and not all of it is reliable. Overall, technology helps most when people know how to judge sources carefully.
items.vi: Thảo luận công nghệ làm việc ra quyết định dễ hơn hay khó hơn.

audio.t: Brindle Hill Pottery Studio, good evening. How can I help you?
Hello. I saw your leaflet at the library and I would like to enrol on one of your evening courses.
Of course. We run three at the moment: Introduction to Stoneware, Hand Building for Beginners and Glazing Techniques. Have you worked with clay before?
Only at school, a very long time ago. I think the stoneware one sounds right, because I would like to learn to make proper dinner plates and bowls.
Lovely. That course runs on Thursday evenings. There is also a Tuesday group, but it is full until the summer.
Thursday suits me fine. How long does the course last?
It is eight weeks, with two hours each week. Some people ask for ten, but we find eight is enough to cover the basics.
And when does the next one begin?
On the fourth of March. It was going to be the eleventh, but we brought it forward because the kilns are being serviced later that month.
Perfect. What does it cost?
The fee is one hundred and eighty-five dollars. That includes the use of all our tools and the firing of your finished pieces.
Does that cover the clay as well?
Not quite. Materials are charged separately. It used to be twenty-five dollars, but the price of clay has gone up, so it is now thirty-five.
That seems fair. Can I pay today by card?
Yes, I can take your details now. May I have your surname?
It is Wexcombe. That is W-E-X-C-O-M-B-E.
Thank you, Mr Wexcombe. And a contact number?
Five five five, zero one eight three.

Five five five zero one eight three. Thank you. One more thing: you do not need gloves, and we supply towels, but we do not provide aprons, so please bring one, and wear shoes you do not mind getting dirty.
Good to know. And where exactly are you?
We are on Mill Lane, in the old warehouse next to the bakery. You cannot miss it, because of the smell of fresh bread. Parking is free in the evening.
Great, thank you very much.

Of course. We run three at the moment: Introduction to Stoneware, Hand Building for Beginners and Glazing Techniques. Have you worked with clay before?
Only at school, a very long time ago. I think the stoneware one sounds right, because I would like to learn to make proper dinner plates and bowls.
Lovely. That course runs on Thursday evenings. There is also a Tuesday group, but it is full until the summer.
Thursday suits me fine. How long does the course last?
It is eight weeks, with two hours each week. Some people ask for ten, but we find eight is enough to cover the basics.
And when does the next one begin?
On the fourth of March. It was going to be the eleventh, but we brought it forward because the kilns are being serviced later that month.
Perfect. What does it cost?
The fee is one hundred and eighty-five dollars. That includes the use of all our tools and the firing of your finished pieces.
Does that cover the clay as well?
Not quite. Materials are charged separately. It used to be twenty-five dollars, but the price of clay has gone up, so it is now thirty-five.
That seems fair. Can I pay today by card?
Yes, I can take your details now. May I have your surname?
It is Wexcombe. That is W-E-X-C-O-M-B-E.
Thank you, Mr Wexcombe. And a contact number?
Five five five, zero one eight three.

Five five five zero one eight three. Thank you. One more thing: you do not need gloves, and we supply towels, but we do not provide aprons, so please bring one, and wear shoes you do not mind getting dirty.
Good to know. And where exactly are you?
We are on Mill Lane, in the old warehouse next to the bakery. You cannot miss it, because of the smell of fresh bread. Parking is free in the evening.
Great, thank you very much.

audio.t: Welcome to the Wrenfield Heritage Walk. My name is Carla, and I will be your guide for the next ninety minutes. Before we set off, a few practical points.

The walk covers about two miles, mostly on flat ground, so you do not need special boots. However, the cobbles near the old market can be very slippery after rain, so please take care there. We will pause halfway at the Weaver's Rest, where tea and coffee are included in your ticket, but cakes are extra.

Wrenfield grew rich in the eighteenth century, not because of wool, as many visitors assume, but because of its position on the river. Barges carried salt and pottery to the coast, and the merchants built the tall brick houses that you will see on Quay Street. Wool came later, and it was the mills of the nineteenth century that brought the biggest growth in population.

Our first stop is the Clock Tower. It was built in 1790 to replace a wooden bell tower that burned down. Many people believe the fire was started by lightning, but the town records show that a candle left in the bell-ringer's room was the real cause.

After that we cross Haldane Bridge. The original bridge was swept away by floods in 1852. The present one is made of iron, and it was paid for by public donations rather than by the council, which at that time had no money to spare.
On Quay Street, look out for the blue plaques. Each one marks the home of someone who helped the town, and the newest honors Edith Marsh, a nurse who opened the first free clinic here in 1904.
The Museum of Wrenfield Life is unfortunately closed for repairs this month, but the exhibition of old photographs has been moved to the library, which is free to enter and open until six.

At the end of the tour we reach Sutton Park. There is an optional extension to the ruined abbey, which adds twenty minutes. I would recommend it if you enjoy views, though the path is steep and not suitable for pushchairs.

Finally, the tour is run entirely by volunteers, and the money you pay goes towards restoring the town's old water pump. If you would like to join us as a guide, we especially need people who can speak French or German, as we have so many visitors from abroad.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. I have read your proposal on the Saltby fishing community. Tell me how the project started.
It began with my grandfather. He fished from Saltby for forty years, and he told me the harbor has changed so much that younger people do not even know what the boats used to carry.
We thought we could record interviews with older fishermen before those memories are lost. At first we also considered analyzing old sales records, but that seemed like too much.
A wise decision. Oral history is valuable, but remember that memory is not a perfect record. What will you do about that?
We plan to compare each account with the harbor logbooks, which are held in the town archive. Where they disagree, we will report both versions.
Good. That is better than simply deciding which is right. Now, how many interviews do you have in mind?
Originally twenty, but I think fifteen is more realistic, since each one will take at least three hours to transcribe.
I agree with fifteen. Quality matters more than quantity, and you only have one semester. How will you find participants?
The harbor office has offered to put up a notice, and my grandfather knows several men who are keen to talk. The risk is that they are all old friends, so they might tell very similar stories.
That is an important point. Try to include a few people from other families and, if possible, one or two women who worked in the processing sheds. Their experience is often overlooked.
We had not thought of that. We could ask at the community center.
Now, about equipment. Will you use your phones?
I wanted to, but Nadia is worried about the sound quality.
The harbor is noisy, so I think we should borrow recorders from the department and interview people at home instead.
Wise. And on ethics: every participant must sign a consent form, and you must say clearly who will hear the recordings. Some people forget what they agreed to years later.
Should we let them check the transcripts?
Yes. It takes more time, but it builds trust, and it catches mistakes in names and dates.
What about the final presentation? We thought of a written report with extracts.

Think about something more creative. A short audio documentary would let your sources speak in their own voices, which a report cannot do. But you will still need a written part, around three thousand words, analyzing what you found.
When is the deadline?
The draft is due on the twelfth of December. Book a meeting with me in week six to discuss your first interviews.
Thank you. We will.

audio.t: Today I want to talk about the chemistry of colour in fireworks. A firework looks like magic, but every colour you see comes from a simple principle. When a metal compound is heated, its atoms absorb energy, and when they release that energy it appears as light of a particular colour.

Inside a shell are small pellets called stars. Each star contains fuel, an oxidizer that supplies oxygen so it can burn quickly, and a metal salt that produces the colour. Different metals give different colours, and a firework designer chooses them very carefully.

Let us start with red. Strontium salts give a deep red, and they are also used in emergency flares. Orange comes from calcium, which gives a softer glow than strontium. Yellow is produced by sodium, and it is so bright that even a tiny amount can hide the other colours.

Green is created by barium compounds. Blue is the hardest colour of all. The copper compounds that make blue light break down if the temperature goes above about one thousand degrees Celsius, so the mixture must burn at a lower temperature than other colours. That is why a truly deep blue is rare.

Silver and white sparks come from burning metal powders. Aluminium and magnesium burn at extremely high temperatures and give a dazzling white light. Titanium is used for bright silver sparks that fall slowly. Gold sparks are usually made from fine iron filings or charcoal.

The shape of the explosion is also planned. Stars are packed around a central charge called the burst charge. If the stars are arranged in a ring, the pattern in the sky is a ring. Heart shapes and smiley faces use stars glued onto cardboard templates inside the shell.

Timing matters too. A fuse burns for a few seconds while the shell climbs, and the burst charge fires when it reaches its highest point, usually between one hundred and two hundred meters above the ground for a small shell. Large shells can climb much higher.

Now the smoke. The explosion produces gases and fine particles, and on a still night the smoke can hang in the air and spoil the view. Modern designers are therefore replacing some chemicals with ones that produce less smoke.

Finally, safety and the environment. Some metal salts, particularly those containing perchlorate, can pollute water, so researchers are developing cleaner mixtures. Nitrogen-rich fuels are one promising option, because they burn with much less smoke and leave fewer harmful residues.

The shape of the explosion is also planned. Stars are packed around a central charge called the burst charge. If the stars are arranged in a ring, the pattern in the sky is a ring. Heart shapes and smiley faces use stars glued onto cardboard templates inside the shell.

Timing matters too. A fuse burns for a few seconds while the shell climbs, and the burst charge fires when it reaches its highest point, usually between one hundred and two hundred meters above the ground for a small shell. Large shells can climb much higher.

Now the smoke. The explosion produces gases and fine particles, and on a still night the smoke can hang in the air and spoil the view. Modern designers are therefore replacing some chemicals with ones that produce less smoke.

Finally, safety and the environment. Some metal salts, particularly those containing perchlorate, can pollute water, so researchers are developing cleaner mixtures. Nitrogen-rich fuels are one promising option, because they burn with much less smoke and leave fewer harmful residues.

audio.t: Today I want to talk about the chemistry of colour in fireworks. A firework looks like magic, but every colour you see comes from a simple principle. When a metal compound is heated, its atoms absorb energy, and when they release that energy it appears as light of a particular colour.

Inside a shell are small pellets called stars. Each star contains fuel, an oxidizer that supplies oxygen so it can burn quickly, and a metal salt that produces the colour. Different metals give different colours, and a firework designer chooses them very carefully.

Let us start with red. Strontium salts give a deep red, and they are also used in emergency flares. Orange comes from calcium, which gives a softer glow than strontium. Yellow is produced by sodium, and it is so bright that even a tiny amount can hide the other colours.

items.text:
The Inner Ecosystem
A. The human intestine hosts somewhere between thirty and forty trillion microbial cells, a population roughly equal in number to the body's own cells. For most of the twentieth century, medicine regarded these organisms chiefly as passengers or, at worst, as a source of infection. That view began to change in the 2000s, when cheap DNA sequencing allowed researchers to identify bacteria that could never be grown in a laboratory dish. Surveys revealed that a single gut may contain over a thousand species, that two healthy adults share fewer than half of them, and that the community's composition is shaped by diet, geography, medication and, above all, the first years of life.
B. Infancy appears to be the formative period. Babies are born with a nearly sterile gut and acquire their first microbes from the mother during birth and from breast milk, which contains sugars that the infant cannot digest but that nourish particular bacteria. A team led by Dr. Ilse Varnholt at Kessmark University followed 900 children from birth to the age of seven. Those delivered by caesarean section, or given antibiotics in their first six months, carried a less varied community at age three. Crucially, however, most of these differences had faded by school age, suggesting that the early microbiome is more resilient than alarmist reports implied. The researchers did note that a small subgroup, whose diversity never recovered, had higher rates of childhood asthma, although they cautioned that their data could not show that one caused the other.
C. What do the microbes actually do? Their most obvious service is digestion. Humans lack the enzymes to break down many plant fibers, so bacteria ferment them, releasing short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells lining the colon and help to regulate inflammation. Gut microbes also manufacture vitamin K and several B vitamins, and they help to train the immune system to distinguish harmless substances from genuine threats. Perhaps most intriguing is the evidence of a two-way conversation with the brain. Around ninety percent of the body's serotonin is produced in the gut, and although this chemical does not cross directly into the brain, signals traveling along the vagus nerve appear to carry information about the state of the intestine upwards.
D. This "gut-brain axis" has attracted the greatest enthusiasm, and the greatest exaggeration. In one widely reported experiment, mice that received gut bacteria from anxious donors became more timid themselves. Yet a mouse's gut differs markedly from a human's, and laboratory animals are raised on uniform diets that no person eats. A review by the Haldane Institute in 2023 examined forty-one human trials of probiotic supplements for depression and found measurable benefits in only a handful, most of them small and short-lived. The reviewers concluded that the field's promise was real but that its commercial claims ran well ahead of the proof.
E. Part of the difficulty is that a "healthy microbiome" has proved remarkably hard to define. Early studies hoped to identify an ideal set of species, in the way that a healthy cholesterol level can be specified. Instead, researchers discovered that quite different communities can perform the same functions, much as different orchestras can play the same symphony. Many scientists have therefore shifted their attention from which species are present to what the community is doing: which genes are active and which compounds it produces. Diversity remains a useful rough indicator, but it is no longer treated as a score to be maximized, since some very diverse communities are found in people with chronic bowel disease.
F. The most dramatic clinical success so far is fecal microbiota transplantation, in which a preparation from a healthy donor is introduced into a patient's bowel. For recurrent infections with Clostridioides difficile, which can persist after repeated courses of antibiotics, the procedure cures about eight patients in ten, a rate far higher than for standard drugs. Its use for other conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease, has been much less convincing. Regulators also worry about safety: in one reported case, a recipient developed a drug-resistant infection from an inadequately screened donor, and screening rules have since been tightened.
G. Looking ahead, several groups are moving away from wholesale transplants toward defined mixtures of a few dozen strains, which can be manufactured to a consistent standard. Others are exploring personalized nutrition. In a trial of 800 volunteers, researchers found that individuals' blood sugar responses to identical meals varied widely, and that an algorithm incorporating gut bacteria predicted these responses better than simply counting carbohydrates. Even so, the algorithm explained only part of the variation, and nobody yet knows whether following its advice improves long-term health. For now, the most robust recommendation is also the least glamorous: eat a wide range of plant foods.

items.text:
Buildings That Heal
A. Few people would dispute that a gloomy, noisy room affects mood, yet the study of how the built environment influences health has only recently moved beyond intuition. The roots of the field lie in nineteenth-century hospital reform, when campaigners argued that ventilation and daylight reduced infection, a claim later supported by the discovery of airborne transmission. Modern research asks subtler questions: not merely whether buildings can harm us, but whether particular design features can measurably improve recovery, concentration and social contact, and by how much, for which groups of people, and under what conditions.
B. The best-known evidence concerns views of nature. In a frequently cited study from the 1980s, patients recovering from gallbladder surgery in rooms overlooking trees left the hospital about a day earlier than matched patients whose windows faced a brick wall, and they requested fewer strong painkillers. Critics pointed out that the study involved only a few dozen patients in a single hospital. A replication at Marrowfield Hospital, led by Dr. Tomas Ekwueme, used 600 patients across four wards and found a smaller but still significant effect: discharge about six hours earlier. Ekwueme argued that the shrinking of the effect did not discredit the original finding. On the contrary, he said, a modest benefit that survives larger testing is more credible than a spectacular one that has never been challenged.
C. Light is a second recurring theme. Exposure to bright daylight in the morning helps to set the body's internal clock, and offices with poor natural light have been associated with disturbed sleep among staff. In a study of one hundred office workers, those seated near windows slept on average 46 minutes longer each night than those in the interior. Yet the same study could not rule out that people with better sleeping habits simply chose desks beside windows, or that senior staff, who tend to be less stressed, were given them. Architects therefore tend to treat such findings as grounds for further trials rather than as rules.
D. Noise and layout also matter. Open-plan offices, introduced in the hope of encouraging collaboration, have often been criticized for achieving the opposite. When an engineering firm called the Halvorsen Group moved 150 employees from private rooms to a single open floor, face-to-face conversation fell by roughly seventy percent, while the volume of e-mail rose sharply. Employees seemed to respond to the lack of privacy by withdrawing behind headphones and screens. The finding is often read as proof that open-plan design is a mistake, but the researchers were more guarded. The new floor had no quiet rooms at all, and a different arrangement, they suggested, might have produced a different result.
E. Housing offers perhaps the most persuasive natural experiments, because tenants are often allocated flats by waiting list rather than by choice, which reduces the problem of self-selection. At Linden Court, a redeveloped estate in the city of Tarnow, residents were placed in apartments arranged around shared courtyards instead of along the long corridors typical of earlier blocks. Five years later, tenants reported knowing on average twice as many neighbors, and loneliness among older residents was a third lower than on a comparable corridor-style estate nearby. The designers had deliberately positioned entrances so that residents' paths crossed, a tactic they called "engineered encounter". Some residents nevertheless complained that the courtyards felt too public, which shows that the same feature can seem supportive to one person and intrusive to another.
F. This variation points to the central difficulty of the field. People differ in age, culture and temperament, and a space that one person finds calming another finds dull. Moreover, design is rarely the only influence: a beautifully planned clinic with understaffed wards will not heal patients faster. Researchers therefore increasingly combine measurements such as heart rate, sleep tracking and questionnaires with detailed accounts of how occupants actually use a space, hoping to separate the effect of design from the effects of staffing, income and routine.
G. Even so, a growing number of public bodies now require "health impact assessments" for large developments, and some funders insist that hospitals be designed on the basis of evidence rather than fashion. Critics fear that this will produce standardized buildings that tick every box but lack character. Supporters reply that the evidence is better treated as a set of questions than as a formula, leaving architects free to answer them in different ways. Whichever view prevails, the idea that a building is merely a neutral container for human activity is unlikely to return.

items.text:
The Quiet Decline of Pollinators
A. Of the hundred or so crop species that supply most of the world's food, roughly three quarters rely to some degree on animal pollination, and the proportion is higher among the fruits, nuts and vegetables that provide many of our vitamins. Public attention has focused on the honeybee, yet it is only one of more than twenty thousand bee species, and bees are joined by hoverflies, moths, beetles and wasps and, in warmer regions, by bats and birds. Since the early 2000s, reports of falling numbers have multiplied, and the phrase "pollinator crisis" now appears in policy documents across the world. The reality, as researchers are quick to point out, is both more uncertain and more nuanced than the headlines suggest.
B. The strongest evidence comes from long-running surveys in temperate regions. In the Veldt Valley, volunteers have recorded bee sightings since 1950, and about forty percent of the species logged in that first decade were absent from the most recent decade's records. Even this survey, however, illustrates the problem with the data. Volunteers favored accessible sites near towns, observers' skill and enthusiasm varied, and rare species are by definition hard to spot. For most of the tropics, where diversity is greatest, there are simply no historical records at all, and the great majority of species have never been assessed. The honeybee, meanwhile, gives a misleading impression, because global colony numbers have actually risen over the past fifty years, the growth of beekeeping in Asia and Africa having more than offset losses in Europe and North America. Managed hives say little about the fate of the wild species that pollinate many crops more efficiently.
C. Most scientists identify four principal pressures: loss of habitat, exposure to pesticides, parasites and disease, and climate change. Intensive farming removed hedgerows and flower-rich meadows, leaving bees with fewer places to feed and nest. A class of insecticides known as neonicotinoids, applied to seeds and absorbed into the whole plant, can reach pollen and nectar, and even sub-lethal doses have been shown to impair navigation and reduce egg laying. The Varroa mite, which feeds on honeybees and spreads viruses, has traveled across continents with the trade in colonies. Warming temperatures, finally, may disturb the timing between flowering and the emergence of insects, so that bees wake before the flowers on which they depend.
D. What makes the problem hard to solve is that these pressures seldom act alone. In experiments led by Dr. Sunil Barrowman, colonies of bumblebees were exposed to a low dose of pesticide, to a restricted diet, or to both. Either stress alone reduced colony growth only slightly, by about ten percent; together they halved it. Such interactions mean that a pesticide judged safe in a laboratory trial, where insects are well fed and healthy, may prove harmful in a field where food is scarce. Regulatory testing has been slow to reflect this finding.
E. The economic stakes are often quoted in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but economists urge caution. Such figures, they note, imagine a world in which all pollinators vanish overnight, which no one expects, and they ignore the ability of farmers to adapt. Some already have. In the Tessaly orchards, where wild pollinators collapsed during the 1990s, growers now pay workers to pollinate apple blossom by hand with small brushes, at a cost that has more than doubled the labor bill per hectare. The example is sometimes used as evidence that humans can replace the insects; it is more often read as a warning of what the replacement costs.
F. Remedies are under debate. Sowing wildflower strips along field margins has become the commonest policy, and a trial on eighty farms found that the strips tripled bee numbers within two years. Yet the benefit to crop yields was small and took four years to appear, which makes the strips a hard sell to farmers who lose productive land. Some ecologists argue that restoring habitat across entire landscapes would achieve more than scattered strips, although this requires a degree of coordination that individual farmers rarely have. Technological alternatives, such as drones carrying pollen, attract headlines but remain far from competing with insects: a single bee visits hundreds of flowers an hour at almost no cost.
G. A further complication is that not all pollinators are losing. Generalist species, which feed on many kinds of flower and nest in varied places, have adapted well to towns and farmland, and in some areas they have become more common. The losers are the specialists, which depend on a single plant family or a narrow habitat, and these are precisely the species that pollinate many wild plants. A landscape could therefore show healthy bee numbers while losing the diversity on which the resilience of the ecosystem depends. For this reason, many researchers argue that uncertainty is a poor excuse for delay: it is cheaper to protect pollinators now than to rebuild a service that, once lost, would be difficult to replace.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visits, in thousands, to four types of cultural venue in the city of Marlow in 2000, 2012 and 2024, together with the average ticket price in 2024.
Cinemas: 410 in 2000; 520 in 2012; 295 in 2024; average ticket $11.
Museums: 180 in 2000; 240 in 2012; 365 in 2024; average ticket $6.
Theaters: 120 in 2000; 135 in 2012; 150 in 2024; average ticket $28.
Libraries: 560 in 2000; 430 in 2012; 280 in 2024; free entry.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the number of visits to four kinds of cultural venue in Marlow in 2000, 2012 and 2024, and shows what a ticket cost in 2024.
Overall, museums and theaters attracted more visits over the period, whereas libraries suffered a steady decline. Cinemas rose at first and then fell sharply.
Libraries were the most popular venue in 2000, with 560 thousand visits, but the figure dropped to 430 thousand in 2012 and to only 280 thousand in 2024. Cinemas followed a different pattern: visits grew from 410 thousand to 520 thousand by 2012, before falling to 295 thousand, which was lower than the starting figure.
Museums, by contrast, doubled their audience, from 180 thousand in 2000 to 365 thousand in 2024, and by the end they had overtaken both cinemas and libraries. Theaters grew only modestly, from 120 thousand to 150 thousand, which made them the least visited venue throughout.
In 2024, theaters were by far the most expensive, at $28 a ticket, compared with $11 for cinemas and $6 for museums, while libraries were free. This suggests that price alone does not explain popularity.
items.vi: Mô tả số liệu: nêu xu hướng chính (bảo tàng tăng, thư viện giảm, rạp chiếu phim tăng rồi giảm), so sánh các địa điểm, nhắc đến giá vé và có câu tổng quan.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 2. Nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này.

items.q: In many countries, young people are spending less time reading books for pleasure than they did in the past. What are the causes of this trend, and what can be done to encourage young people to read more? Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
In many countries, fewer teenagers now pick up a book in their free time. This essay will examine the main reasons for this change and suggest some practical remedies.
The most obvious cause is competition from screens. A phone offers games, videos and messages that arrive instantly, while a novel demands patience and sustained attention. Since young people can carry entertainment everywhere, reading must compete with options that are designed to be hard to put down. A second cause is pressure at school. When reading is linked mainly to exams and assignments, students may come to see it as work rather than pleasure, and they stop when the homework ends. Finally, busy family routines leave less time for the shared reading that once helped children to form the habit.
There are several ways to respond. First, schools could set aside regular time for free reading, allowing students to choose their own books instead of following a fixed list. Choice matters, because a teenager who finds a story that matches his or her interests is far more likely to continue. Second, public libraries can become more attractive by offering quiet spaces, book clubs and digital loans, so that the habit of reading does not feel old-fashioned. Third, parents can set an example by reading themselves and by limiting screens during the evening, which also helps with sleep.
In conclusion, the decline in reading for pleasure results mainly from digital distractions, school pressure and lack of time. If schools, libraries and families work together to make reading enjoyable and easy to fit into daily life, many more young people will rediscover it.
items.vi: Bài luận nêu nguyên nhân (màn hình, áp lực học tập, thiếu thời gian) và giải pháp (đọc tự chọn ở trường, thư viện hấp dẫn hơn, cha mẹ làm gương), có mở bài và kết luận.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the examiner's questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I do enjoy cooking, mostly because it helps me relax after school. I often prepare simple dishes for my family at the weekend, and they always say it tastes good.
items.vi: Nói em có thích nấu ăn không, kèm lý do và ví dụ.

items.q: How do you usually travel around your town?
items.sample: I usually take the bus because it is cheap and there is a stop near my house. When the weather is nice, I sometimes cycle instead, which is faster in the city center.
items.vi: Nói phương tiện em hay dùng để đi lại và vì sao.

items.q: What kind of music do you listen to?
items.sample: I listen to many kinds of music, but I mostly like calm piano music because it helps me concentrate when I am studying. At parties, however, I prefer something more lively.
items.vi: Nói thể loại nhạc em nghe và lý do.

items.q: Is there a place in your town where you like to spend time alone?
items.sample: Yes, there is a small park near the river where I like to sit. It is very quiet in the late afternoon, and I can read or just think there because few people go.
items.vi: Nói về nơi yên tĩnh em thích ở một mình.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1-2 phút.

items.q: Describe a documentary or book that taught you something new. You should say: what it was; what you learned from it; why you chose it; and explain how it changed the way you think.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a documentary about the deep ocean that I watched last year. I chose it because my science teacher recommended it, and I was curious about animals that live where there is no sunlight. It was far more interesting than I expected. The most surprising thing I learned was that many creatures in the deep sea make their own light, and that they use it to hide, to hunt and even to communicate. Before that I had imagined the bottom of the ocean as an empty, dark desert. The film showed me that it is full of life, and that scientists still know less about it than about the surface of the moon. Another thing I learned was how fragile these habitats are, because fishing nets and pollution can reach very deep places. The documentary changed the way I think about nature, because I now realize that important discoveries are still waiting to be made. It also made me want to study biology at university, and since then I have read several books about marine animals. I would recommend it to anyone who thinks science is boring, because the pictures are beautiful and the story is easy to follow.
items.vi: Mô tả một phim tài liệu/sách: tên, điều học được, lý do chọn và nó thay đổi cách nghĩ như thế nào; nói đủ các ý trên thẻ.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss these more abstract questions with the examiner.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng hơn với giám khảo.

items.q: Why do some people prefer to learn from videos rather than from books?
items.sample: I think many people prefer videos because they combine pictures, sound and explanation, so difficult ideas are easier to understand. Books, however, usually give more detail and encourage people to think slowly, so they are better for subjects that need deep concentration.
items.vi: Giải thích vì sao nhiều người thích học qua video: dễ hiểu, trực quan; sách thì chi tiết hơn.

items.q: Do you think the information people find online is generally reliable?
items.sample: Not always. Some online information is reliable because it comes from experts, but a lot of it is written by people who want to sell something or who have not checked their facts. I think people should compare several sources before they believe anything, especially on health or science topics.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm về độ tin cậy của thông tin trên mạng và cách kiểm tra nguồn.

items.q: How might education change in the next twenty years?
items.sample: I expect technology to play a bigger role in education, with more online lessons and programs that adapt to each student. However, I do not think it will replace teachers, because students still need someone to motivate them and to explain ideas in a personal way.
items.vi: Dự đoán giáo dục thay đổi: công nghệ nhiều hơn nhưng vẫn cần giáo viên.
